TNA new edition is always a certain index of success achieved. Reading Saint Augustine is a felt need today. The torturous and dynamic restlessness of modern consciousness, with its tragic sense of life in the hopeless search for truth and in perennial dialogue with interiority, can find in Saint Augustine the peaceful grove of a constructive idealism, of far-reaching metaphysical and theological scope, of authentic transcendence to the divine. Ortega y Gasset reads, in the last year of his earthly life, our version of De Trinitate, and is enthralled by the suggestive word, filled with Augustan emotion. It is significant to note how, of all the writings of the Hiponense Doctor with dense doctrinal content, published by the LIBRARY OF CHRISTIAN AUTHORS, it is precisely i'l De Trinitate that is the first to be sold out. This new edition substantially coincides with the first, since neither critics nor scholars have raised any objections. In a few passages our version has been polished with diligence and care, counting the words to adjust them to the quality and condition they have in the original. I wish this second edition short life and eternal fame. Br. Luis ARIAS.

The first known work with the title De Trinitate is authored by Novatian 2 i. Clarity, method, elegance, are the predominant qualities of this Latin writer. At the same time as De Trinitate, he brings forward his great philosophy of history in The City of God, and his masterful Commentaries on Genesis, and his profound treatises on the Gospel of Saint John. He therefore gives De Trinitate a hand whenever other more pressing duties € that cannot be postponed demand his attention 21. The style of this work is not uniform. Three decades weigh heavily on a man's life, and at the peak of sixty-two years the cadences of Ciceronian prose are abandoned for the seasoned fruits of thought. But Agustín, as a writer, always has an unmistakable stamp. He lives what he writes, and his warm verb is a reflection of his passionate and restless soul. The Trinity God is not a merely speculative truth for him, but a living reality already known. He internalizes theology, and his word springs spontaneously upon contact with his loves. Sometimes you feel the burning breath of fatigue in the face of the arduous work to express with the verbum oris the intimate verb that bubbles in your thoughts. We feel the giant's effort to organize the rich flow of his inspiration, at the touch of God's light, along the serene channel of a peaceful flow. A difficult undertaking, because the human word does not always adjust to thought, and thought is infinitely distanced from God. Compared with the writers of his time, Mario Victorinus, Macrobius, Claudian, Augustine stands out for the depth of his knowledge, the density of his thought, dilated like the sea, and for the beauty of his prose, sometimes solemn as in the best classical periods, sometimes simple, meticulous and without artifice; now drastic and impetuous as in Tertullian. As a poet, he is the greatest of his century among the Fathers, in Norden's phrase 22. It is necessary to penetrate his spirit in full effervescence to understand the juggling of his word games, which, if in others it is ridiculous presumption, in him it is the right mold of his genius. * * *

ANALYSIS OF THE WORK Summarizing the content of this work, deep as the sea, where the tradition of the past and the thought, dense in originalities, of the author, the teachings of the Church and the rational search for the mystery come together in a friendly embrace, an undertaking is risky and not without danger. We will carefully avoid falsifying Augustine's orthodox thought, following in this quick outline the common thread of the De Trinitate, avoiding unnecessary repetitions and trying to group similar matters together. UNITY AND TRINITY

The starting point of the Trinitarian doctrine in Augustine is the unity of essence. The creed in unum Deum of the council of Nicaea. From this source principle flow the necessary consequences of the divine hypostases. The skill lies, then, in avoiding heterodox modalism, making the Trinity of Catholic dogma emerge from this essence. In the light of the Scriptures, the existence of the Trinity in one God is solidly demonstrated. And it is here where Greek and Latin thought accentuate their differences in the words of certain modern writers. In the visual approach to the problem, Augustine sees in God an essence that is personalized; The Greeks see a person, that of the Father, who becomes essential. Augustine conceives the essence of God as subsisting in three distinct persons by relationship of origin, while the Greek Fathers see how God, by realizing himself as a person, becomes tripersonalized. This, as interesting as one may want to pretend, gives the impression of a play on words. Deep down, Greeks and Latins profess the same faith in a Trinity God. This is a mysterious way of the subsistence of unity in plurality, but the divine Scriptures attest to the fact. There is only one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Some shy people feel torture when they hear it said that the Father is God, the Son is God and that the Holy Spirit is God, and the three are one God. However, only the voice of the Father was heard on high, only the Son took flesh in the immaculate wombs of a Virgin mother, and only the Holy Spirit was seen in the form of a dove on the flowery banks of the Jordan. THE IMAGE OF THE TRINITY IN MAN The WII book is like an arch stretched between the rule of faith and speculation, rich in brilliant intuitions of the wonderful world of the soul. In this second part, Augustine is concerned with elevating hearts towards the sublime goal of the Trinity by following the traces that God has left behind in his footsteps, which are vestiges of his dynamism, relics of his omnipotence, gifts of his goodness. The African thinker, who only longs for the knowledge of God and the soul, advances towards the end of his desire through the sunny rooms of his spirit x. The route to follow in the search is self-knowledge and prayer. His sight, "avid and loving in following the traces of the divine image in the human soul, finalizes the synthesis of his own philosophical, theological and mystical thought" 2. But before penetrating the recesses of the mind, he rests his inner gaze on the peak of the climbed eminences, contemplating the path traveled in previous books. Note with loving complacency how in the exalted Trinity two persons are not greater than one of them. The greatness of a being lies in its truth: the truer being is greater. The intelligible and immutable does not admit degrees in truth, since it is eternal. Where greatness is the truth, to be greater is to be truer. Well, the Father and the Son together are no more true than the Father or the Son in particular. Therefore the two united are not greater than one of them. And the Holy Spirit is as true and, therefore, as great as the Father and the Son, and the Trinity is not greater or truer than each of the persons that compose it 3. The word truth in Augustine's pen acquires a hierarchy of efficient reality, and is synonymous with intelligible, in essences, in relationships or in numbers *, not phenomenal. It is also urgent to note here the marked dissimilarities that exist between the image and the divine model if we are to avoid the precipice 73. The differences are large and obvious. Man remembers, loves and understands through his faculties, but it is neither his memory, nor his understanding, nor his will, but rather he possesses these three things. Any man has these three powers, but he is not any of these three things. In divine simplicity there are three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and these three persons are one God. 'As a respite from arduous study and a relief for the pilgrim of the trinities, Augustine tries to find in the outer man, who crumbles under the harsh blow of time, an effigy of the Trinity, coarser, yes, but also easier to discern. This explains why in book XI he orients his search towards bodily vision. From the internal world we look to the external world. It is the perspective of the visible over the intelligible. The same familiarity with external objects makes us more pleasant to study them. It is not necessary—it would be a painful task—to interrogate the five senses for what we come seeking; An attentive and detailed examination of what is manifested in vision is enough, as this is the noblest sense of the body and the one that offers the most analogies with the vision of thought. In bodily vision, the investigator of the divine mysteries recognizes three realities: the visible object, for example, a flame or a stone, with real existence before the vision occurs; Then comes vision, which did not exist before seeing the object; and, finally, the attention of the spirit, which makes the gaze rest on the corporeal object. We have, then, a visible body, its form printed on the retina and, as a third element, the union of both by a volitional act of the viewer. Three realities of a different nature, since the visible object is of a very different substance than the visual organ, where vision takes place. This is nothing but the meaning informed by the visible image. The test is simple. Without the visible object, there is certainly no vision, but the sense of Sight can exist. And, on the other hand, the attention of the spirit, which applies meaning to the object, differs by nature from the body, since it is spirit, while the eyes are corporeal members and the object is also a body. This explains the ease of their numerical distinction 75. But, although disparate in nature, the visible body, sight and attention of the spirit are tempered in a certain unity: vision. CHAPTER XV THE FIFTEEN BOOKS ON THE TRINITY

1. Over the space of some years (16) I wrote fifteen books about the Trinity, which is God. But without yet completing the twelfth, by retaining them longer than I could endure the impatience of those who strongly desired to possess them, they were stolen from me, less polished than they should have been and could be if I wanted to publish them. When I knew this, since some copies had remained in my possession, I decided not to publish them, but to retain them and report what happened in some other booklet of mine. Still young (400), I began these my books on the Trinity, who is the supreme and true God, and in my old age I published them (416). I ceased my work when I discovered that my books had been stolen from me before finishing my work and before I could correct them by means of a thorough retraction, as I desired. Publishing my complete work was my decision, and not book by book, because, as the search progresses, those that follow are linked in close connection with the previous ones. Being impossible to carry out my purpose successfully because of the friends into whose hands my books had reached, without my wanting it, I interrupted my dictation and thought I would regret the fact in my other writings and thus make known how my work had not been published by me, but had been taken from me before it seemed worthy of seeing the public light. But, requested by the insistent requests of many brothers and, above all, Obliged by your command, I decided to continue this painful work and finish it with the help of the Lord. Corrected, not according to my desire, but according to my possibilities, so that they do not turn out to be too dissimilar to the first ones, which were stolen from me and are now in the hands of men, I now send them to your venerable paternity through our very beloved son and codeacon, authorizing everyone to read and transcribe them. Had I followed my plan, even retaining the same doctrinal background, my exposition would have been clearer and simpler, always keeping in mind the abstruse nature of the subject and the meagerness of my strength. There are those who have their proem, my first four or five books and the twelfth without a notable part of its end; but if this edition comes to their knowledge, they will correct, if they want and can, all these deficiencies. I beg you to order this letter to be placed, separately, yes, but at the front of my books. Be healthy. Pray for me.

In order, therefore, to purify the human soul from these falsehoods, the Holy Scripture, adapting itself to our parvity, did not avoid any human word with the attempt to elevate, in gentle gradation, our well-cultivated understanding to the sublime heights of the divine mysteries. Thus, when speaking of God, he uses expressions taken from the corporeal world and says: Cover me in the shadow of your wings. And he even likes to usurp countless locutions from the immaterial world, not to signify what God is in himself, but because it was convenient to express himself in this way. On the contrary, regarding non-existent things, Scripture generally refrains from using expressions that create enigmas or illuminate sentences. With similes taken from creation, divine Scripture usually forms children's pastimes with the intention of arousing, through its steps, in the weak a passionate love for higher realities, abandoning the lower ones.

Therefore, with the help of the Lord, our God, I will try to answer, as far as I can, the question that my adversaries ask, namely, that the Trinity is urf alone, unique and true God, and how correctly it is said, believed and understood that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are of the same essence or substance; so that, not mocked with our excuses, but convinced by experience, they are persuaded of the existence of the Supreme Good, visible to pure souls, and of its ineffable incomprehensibility, because the weak penetration of human intelligence cannot fix its gaze on the sparkling brilliance of light if it is not strengthened by the justice of faith. First it is necessary to prove, based on the authority of the Holy Scriptures, whether this is our faith. Then, God willing and helping us, I will address my response to these disputing garrules, more puffed up than capable, sick with great danger, perhaps helping them to find a truth of which they cannot doubt, and forcing them, in what they could find, to quarantine the penetration and acuity of their intelligence rather than doubt the truth and rectitude of our disquisitions. And if there is in them a spark of love or fear of God, let them return to the order and principle of faith, experiencing within themselves the salutary influence of the medicine of the faithful existing in the holy Church, so that well-cultivated piety may heal the weakness of their intelligence and may perceive the unchangeable truth, and thus their reckless audacity may not precipitate them into opinions of deceptive falsehood. And I will not be ashamed to investigate when I doubt, nor will I be ashamed to learn when I err. Human reason, abandoned to its own forces, is powerless to prove with convincing arguments the existence of the mystery of mysteries. The subtle disquisitions of Augustine's penetrating genius—he himself warns us—will not, therefore, be apodictic demonstrations, but perspectives of the ineffable. Cf. 5. Therefore, whoever reads this, if he is certain, advance in my company; Inquire with me, if you doubt; Come to my field when you recognize your error, and straighten my steps when I go astray. Thus we will march, with equal steps, along the paths of charity in search of him of whom it is written: Always seek his face. This is the pious and sure rule that I offer, in the presence of the Lord, our God, to those who read my writings, especially this treatise, where the unity of the Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit is defended, since there is no matter where it is more dangerously destroyed, nor investigated with more effort, or found with greater fruit. He who, while reading, exclaims: "This is not well said, because I do not understand it," criticizes my word, not my faith. The phrase could perhaps be more clear: however, no man has been able to express himself in a way that everyone understands him in everything. He who does not agree with my expression or does not understand it, see if he is capable of understanding other authors more versed in these issues, and if so, close my book, and, if you like, corner it and dedicate your efforts and your time to those who understand. However, do not think that I should remain silent because I do not express myself with the precision and clarity of the authors that he understands. Not all the books that are written circulate in the hands of everyone; and it is possible that some do not have within their reach the writings that are considered most accessible and come across these of ours and are able to understand them. That is why it is useful that certain questions are treated by different authors of identical beliefs, with different styles, so that the same truth becomes known to many, some through this channel, others through that. But no one regrets not understanding my language because they were never able to understand such things, even though they are presented with acuity and diligence. They try to advance in their desires and studies, but do not try to make me silence with their complaints and outrages.

I truly believe that some, more slow-witted, will think in certain passages of my books that I said what I did not say or that I did not say what I said. Who does not know that their error is not to be imputed to me if, in following my steps, while I am forced to walk along an obscure and impracticable path, they do not understand me and deviate until they find themselves in error, if no one can rightly attribute to the sacred authorities of the divine books the multiple and varied errors of the heretics, when they all turn to the Scriptures to defend their fallacious and erroneous opinions? The law of Christ, with the gentlest rule, that is, charity, openly admonishes me and orders me to prefer to be rebuked by him who lambasts error rather than the flattery of him who praises it, when men believe that I have defended in my books some error that I do not defend, some please and others displease. Although unjustly, since it is not my opinion, with just anger the error is reproached by the former; while, on the contrary, I am not rightly praised by him who judges that I defend what the truth condemns, nor is a doctrine rightly praised that the truth reproaches. 7. How many Catholic interpreters of the divine books of the Old and New Testaments I have been able to read, prior to me in the speculation about the Trinity, which is God, teach, according to the tenor of the Scriptures, that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, of the same and identical substance, insinuate, in inseparable equality, the divine oneness, and, consequently, they are not three gods, but one God. And although the Father begot a Son, the Son is not the Father; and although the Son is begotten by the Father, the Father is not the Son; and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but the Spirit of the Father and the Son, the Father and the Son coequal and belonging to the triune unity. However, the Trinity was not born of the Virgin Mary, nor was it crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate, nor was it resurrected on the third day. nor ascended into heaven, but the Son alone; nor did the Trinity descend in the form of a dove upon Jesus on the day of his baptism; nor in the solemnity of Pentecost, after the ascension of the Lord, between hurricane winds and roars from heaven. came to rest, in the form of tongues of fire, on the apostles, but only the Holy Spirit. Finally, the Trinity did not say from heaven: You are my Son, when Jesus was baptized by John, or on the mountain when he was in the company of his three disciples, nor when that voice resounded: I have glorified him and I will glorify him again, but it was only the time of the Father, who spoke to his Son, although the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are inseparable in their essence and in their operations. And this is my faith, because it is the Catholic faith.

Consequently, it is very easy to understand how Paul, the Apostle, when saying the only one who possesses immortality, speaks not only of the Father, but of the only God, who is the Trinity itself. Eternal life can never be mortal due to mutability, and for this reason in the words the only immortal is included along with the Father and the Son, because it is eternal life. We ourselves are partakers of eternal life, and, according to our ability, we become immortal. But shared eternal life is one thing and our nature, capable of living eternally thanks to this participation, is another. With these and other similar testimonies of the divine Scriptures, our ancestors, using them with a long hand, refuted, as has been said, the errors and slanders of the heretics, strengthening our faith in the unity and equality of a Triune God. But since many passages of the holy books, because of the incarnation of the Word of God, carried out for our redemption by Jesus Christ, mediator of God and men, intimate and openly demonstrate the superiority of the Father over the Son, mortals erred, and, without diligently investigating the complete series of Scriptures, attributed to the nature that was and is eternal before the incarnation what is said of Christ as man. Those who say that the Son is inferior to the Father support their sentence in the words of the Lord when he says: The Father is greater than I. But the truth shows that in this sense the Son is also inferior to himself. And how can he not be inferior to himself, if he annihilated himself by taking the form of a slave? However, by putting on the form of a slave he did not lose the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father. If, then, he took the form of a servant without losing his divine form—in his form as a servant and in his form as God he is always the only begotten Son of the Father—in his divine form equal to the Father, and in his form as a servant, mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, who does not see that in his form as God he is superior to himself and in his form as a slave he is inferior to himself? With complete reason, Scripture affirms both things: that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. There is no confusion here: he is equal to the Father due to his divine nature, inferior because of his slave nature. And this rule, suitable for resolving any difficulties that occur in Scripture, is taken from a chapter of the Letter of Saint Paul the Apostle to the faithful of Philippi, since this distinction is expressly found there. When you hear the Apostle say: When he says that all things are subject to him, it is clear that he excepts him who subjected them to him, let no one think that it is to be interpreted as if the Father submitted all things to the Son, so that the Son has not subjected everything to his own power. Saint Paul explains his thoughts to those of Philip when he writes: Our home is in heaven, from where we await the Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our vileness, according to his glorious body, by virtue of the power he has to subject all things to himself. Therefore the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable. Otherwise it would not be the Father who subjugated all things, but it would be the Son who subjugated them by consigning to him a ruin free of all principality, all power and all dominion. 20. Our Lord Jesus Christ will consign the kingdom into the hands of God the Father when he leads believers to the contemplation of God, the end of all good actions, eternal rest, perennial joy, without excluding himself or the Holy Spirit. This is what he implies when he says: I will see you again, and your heart will be glad, and no one will be able to take away your joy. Mary, sitting at the feet of the Lord and attentive to his word, is a beautiful image of this joy. Free from all occupation, absorbed in contemplative ecstasy of the Truth, as far as possible in this life, it is an image of our future state in eternity. Martha, her sister, was busy with useful tasks, good, yes, and necessary, but transitory, which must be followed by a sweet rest, while Mary rests in the word of the Lord. And when Martha laments because her sister does not help her, the Lord responds: Mary chose the best part and it will not be taken away from her. He does not affirm that Martha's part is bad, but he calls Mary's part optimal, a part that will not be taken away from her. Marta's, at the service of poverty, ends with need. The reward of transitory good work is stable stillness. In that contemplation, God will be all in all, because nothing can be longed for outside of Him, and his vision is enough to delight us in his joy. This is what the one in whom the Spirit prayed with unspeakable groanings asked. One thing, he says, I asked the Lord, and that I seek: to live in the house of the Lord all the days of my life to enjoy the charm of Yahweh. And he does not separate himself from the Father when he says: The Father loves you, but rather he insinuates and gives us to understand, as I noted above, that, when mentioning one person of the Trinity, it is necessary to always understand the other two. Thus, these words: The Father loves you, must equally be understood of the Son and the Holy Spirit; and not because he does not love us now, since he has not forgiven his own Son and sacrificed him for us, but because he does not love us as we are, but as we will be. Those whom he thus loves in time, he preserves in eternity, when he who now intercedes for us has consigned the kingdom to God the Father. Then you will no longer pray to the Father, because the Father himself loves us. And how can we deserve this love, if not through faith in the promises before the vision comes? Faith will lead us to the vision, because it will love us as it wants us to be, not as it hates us for what we are, since it exhorts and helps us so that we do not always want to be bad.

solution. He who believes in me does not believe in what he sees, and thus his hope does not rest in the creature, but in him who assumed the creature, in which he appears visible to the eyes of mortals; and thus, contemplating by faith Him who is equal to the Father, we can purify our hearts. Therefore, raising the thoughts of believers to the Father, he says: He does not believe in me, but in him who sent me, without intending to separate himself from the Father, who sent him, but it is his desire to believe in Him as he believes in the Father, to whom he is equal in all things. This is formally stated where it says: Believe in God and believe also in me. That is, believe in me as you believe in God, because I and the Father are one God. When Christ says: Do not believe in me, but in him who sent me, he turns his attention away from himself to fix it on the Father, without separating himself from Him. Therefore, when he says: It is not for me to grant it, but for those who have been prepared by my Father, I think it is clear in what sense it is to be interpreted. Apply this same distinction to the sentence: I will not judge, because Christ will judge the living and the dead. But as he must judge, his human power turns to the deity and raises the hearts of mortals to the heights, the end of his coming to earth.

Like this: As the Father has life in himself, he also gave the Son to have life in himself; and this other: The Son can do nothing by himself, except what he sees the Father do. If this last testimony means the inferiority of the Son according to his created form, it would follow that the Father first walked on the waters and washed with saliva and mud the eyes of some other person blind from birth, and so on from what the Son did when he appeared in the flesh among men; Only in this way could he execute these actions who affirmed that he could do nothing except what he sees the Father execute. Who, without being delirious, will dare to reason like this? It remains, then, to admit that these things have been said because of the incommutability of life that exists between the Father and the Son, although the Son receives it from the Father, and that the action of the Father and the Son is indivisible; However, the dynamism of the Son comes from the one from whom he receives the being, that is, from the Father; and thus the Son sees the Father, and precisely because he sees him he is the Son. Seeing the Father means being of the Father; that is, being born of the Father; and to see the Father act is to act together with Him, but never on his own, because he does not have being on his own. For this reason: The Son does what he has to do to the Father, because he is born from the Father. By saying everything and also indicating that his action is inseparable and equal to the action of the Father; but it comes to the Son from the Father. 4. As I began to say, there are testimonies in the Holy Books that it is difficult to discern when they refer to the Son as inferior in his condition as a creature and when the Son as equal to the Father, although born of the Father. In my opinion, given the ambiguous nature of certain expressions, they can be interpreted, without danger of error, in both senses. An example: My doctrine is not mine, but of the one who sent me. It can be understood of the Son in his form as a servant, as we have seen in the previous book, and it can also be understood of the Son in his form of God, in which, born of the Father, he is one with the Father. In his form as God, it is not one reality to be Son and another to be life, because the Son is life; nor is it one thing to be a Son and another to be a doctrine, because He is the doctrine. And just as the words gave life to the Son mean that the Father begot the Son, who is life, so when he says: He gave the Son doctrine, he means that he begot the Son, who is doctrine. That is why Christ says: My doctrine is not mine. but the one who sent me. Which is to say: I was not born of myself, but of him who sent me.

by the Father and his Word. Therefore the Son has been sent by the Father and by the Son, because the Son is the Word of the Father. Who will have such a sacrilegious opinion that he dares to say that the Father made his word temporal, so that his eternal Son could be sent and be manifested in time according to the flesh? The one who was to become human and manifest in time was the Son of God himself, and he was in God from the beginning, as extratemporal Wisdom. Without the beginning of time, in the beginning the Word existed, and the Word was in God, and the Word was God. Without the passage of time the Word existed in Him, and in time the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman. That is to say, it happened in time that the humanized Word appeared to mortals, and he who is timeless and exists in the Word, was born in time. The order of times lacks time in the eternal Wisdom of God. When it pleased the Father and the Son that the Son should appear in mortal flesh, then he who manifests himself in the flesh is properly said to have been sent, and he who does not manifest himself in this carnal envelope is said to be a lie. In fact, the things that pass before the eyes of the body outside of us have their origin in the inner disposition of the spiritual nature; That's why they are called conveniently sent. But that form received from human nature belongs to the person of the Son, not to that of the Father. Hence, when the Father, invisible, together with his invisible Son, makes his Son visible, it is said that he sent him; because if he had made him visible, ceasing to be invisible like the Father, that is, if the invisible substance of the Word had been transformed into a visible creature, he would be, yes, the Son sent, but he does not lie with the Father. But having taken the form of a servant, retaining the unchangeable form of God, it is manifest that the Father and the Son, both invisible, have created what is in the visible Son. That is, the one who is visible was sent by the Father and the Son, who are invisible. Why then does Christ say: I have not come from myself? He affirms this according to the form of a servant, and in this sense he says: I do not play with anyone2. 10.

Prophetic vision is not exhibited to the eyes of the body through material forms, but to the soul, using spiritual images of corporeal beings. Those who saw the dove or the fire saw it with their eyes. Although it is possible to doubt whether that fire was seen in a material or incorporeal image, because of the words used there. It does not say that they saw divided tongues like fire, but: They seemed to them. And the word seem does not always have the meaning of vision 4. In spiritual visions of incorporeal images it is customary to say: "It seems to me"; or: "I saw";...but when a material and tangible being is presented to our sight it is no longer common to say: "It seems to me"; but: "I saw." It is possible, therefore, to discuss how the fire was seen: whether with the inner gaze of the soul or really, with the eyes of the body. However, of the dove that descended in bodily form, no one to this day has doubted that it was seen with the eyes. Nor can we call the Holy Spirit a dove or a fire, nor in the sense that we call the Son a stone, as it is written: The stone was Christ. First of all, sticking to what is written in Genesis, God spoke to man, formed from the slime of the earth; And if we rely on the tropological sense and stick to the letter of the narrative, it seems as if God, to converse with man, had taken on a human appearance. It is true that this is not expressly stated in the inspired book, but it is deduced from the circumstances of the lesson; especially where it is narrated that at sunset Adam heard the voice of God, who was walking through Eden, and, hiding in the shadows, the Lord said to him: Adam, Adam, where are you? Here the character who appears is first called the angel of the Lord and then God. Is the angel the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob? However, regarding the question that concerns us at this moment, I declare myself ignorant to substantiate whether it was the Trinity God who spoke in the midst of those terrible wonders, perceptible to the senses of mortals, on the summit of Sinai, or whether it was the Father or the Son or the Holy Spirit. However, if it is permissible for me to express my feelings timidly and modestly, I would lean in favor of the Holy Spirit; for the Law promulgated on Sinai is said to be written on tables of stone by the finger of God, and we know that this name designates the Holy Spirit in the Gospel. And fifty days are numbered from the sacrifice of the lamb and celebration of the Passover until the day on which these wonders occurred on the summit of Sinai; another fifty from the passion and resurrection of the Lord until the coming of the Holy Spirit, promised by the Son. And at this coming, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, he appeared in tongues of fire and rested on each of them; This passage harmonizes with that of the Exodus: The mountain of Sinai was smoking, because the Lord had descended on it in the midst of fire. He encourages one to engage in works of mercy, he fatigues his body at work until he contracts a serious illness; After consulting the doctors, one affirms that the evil comes from dryness of humors, another from abundance; One says the truth, the other is wrong, but both refer to material and proximate causes. But if we investigate the cause of that lack of humors and it is found in voluntary work, we would have reached a higher cause, since the order comes from the soul and is transmitted to the body that it governs; However, this is not yet the supreme reason. To find it, it is necessary to go back to the immutable Wisdom, which the soul of the wise man serves in charity, and, obedient to its inspirations, has voluntarily applied itself to work. And thus the first and supreme cause of that illness is always the will of God. Let us further suppose that in said unofficial and pious work he has collaborating ministers, without their own will to serve God, but driven by the desire to obtain the reward of their carnal lusts or moved by the hope of being able to avoid bodily discomfort. And if the need to complete his good work also advises the use of donkeys, animated but irrational beings, who cannot contribute to the goodness of the work or move their limbs under the weight of their load stimulated by the knowledge of good, but driven only by their natural instinct of pleasure or pain. Finally, our wise man needs to use in his work beings lacking sensitivity, for example, wheat, wine, oil, clothing, money, codices and similar things. Now I ask: in all these bodies used in that work, animated or inanimate, that move, alter, repair, annihilate, renew and bear the imprint of time and place, what, if not the invisible and unchangeable will of God, is the cause of all these visible mutations, which acts through a right and good soul in which wisdom dwells, using all things: rational, but perverse souls; irrational beings, animated horns, endowed with senses or lacking sensitivity, having previously been used by that good and holy soul, submitted to Him in a pious gift of religion?

This happens at Elias's request, after a long and persistent request. The fact that men even perished from hunger, without even a cloud appearing on the horizon as the servant of God prayed and at that hour, a harbinger of the season, is a patent miracle of divine power, because in a moment and with surprising speed the cataracts of heaven opened. God makes the lightning flash and the thunder roll; But when on the summit of Sinai, in a singular way, this happens, without silencing the rumor of the word, and manifesting a new precept through unmistakable signs, we then find ourselves in the presence of a miracle. And who makes the moisture of the earth rise through the chines of the vine and turns it into exquisite wine, but the God who gives the increase when man plants and waters? But, if at an indication from the Lord the water instantly turns into wine, even the short-sighted confess that it is divine virtue that acts. And who, but God, dresses the bush with the pompous clothing of fronds and flowers? But, when the thyrsus of Aaron the priest flourishes, then it is divinity that in a certain way converses with doubting humanity. All trees and the flesh of all animals have certainly been formed from common earthly matter; But who gives this creative power, if not the one who commanded the earth to germinate and by virtue of this efficient verb governs and acts? But when with instantaneous speed the Lord converts the rod of Moses into a true serpent of common matter, then the miracle arises. It is a changeable thing, yes, but unusual. And who, if not the one who gives this ephemeral serpent existence, animates every living thing according to the need of the moment? 5

12. I see here a difficulty arising in impoverished intelligences; namely: how can these portents be a work of magic? For Pharaoh's magicians made serpents and other similar wonders. This implies that neither the transgressor spirits themselves nor the aerial powers precipitated from the abodes of sublime and ethereal purity in deep darkness, as in a sui generis prison, have any power with their magical arts if it were not granted to them from above. CREATION, EXCLUSIVE WORK OF GOD

13. It is not to be believed that the matter of visible things obeys the will of prevaricating spirits, but rather to God, from whom they receive this power to the extent that the Immutable One judges from his spiritual and exalted throne. Water, fire, earth, serve the criminals condemned to the mines so that they can do whatever they please as long as they are allowed. The evil angels should in no sense be called creators, even if in their name the magicians caused snakes and frogs to be born, resisting the servant of God; because the angels did not create them. They pulsate in the hidden cosmic elements as seeds of all existing things and are born into bodily and visible life. Some are perceptible to our sight in their fruits and animals; others, more mysterious, are like seeds and animals; And so, at the voice of the Creator, the water produced fish and birds, and the earth the first germs according to their kind and the first animals according to their kind. This fertilizing power does not exhaust the germinative power by producing the first beings; It is usually a defect in the environmental conditions that prevents its specific germination. The tiny shoot is like a seed, which, planted in a well-disposed tree, becomes a leafy tree. The seed of this shoot is an even smaller grain, although of the same species and perceptible: even though we cannot see with the naked eye the germinal virtue of this grain, we can always guess it by reason; For if this mysterious virtue did not exist in the elements, what had not been sown in the earth would not sprout in the earth, nor would the seas and the earth have produced an immense multitude of beings without the union of male and female preceding them, beings that grow and propagate even if those first from whom they originate were born without a council of parents. Bees conceive by storing the seminal larvae scattered on the ground with their mouths, ignoring all copulation. The breeder of invisible germs is the Maker

Just as Jacob was not the creator of polychromy in his flocks due to the fact that he had placed striped rods in the watering troughs so that mothers in heat could conceive in his sight. Nor are the sheep creators of the varied colors of their lambs for the reason of retaining in their souls the polychrome fantasies that arose from visual contact with the striped rods, something that could not have happened if the body had not been affected by the principle of life, until making it transmit the color to the tender offspring in its embryonic existence. And whether the influence is mutual, whether the soul influences the body or the body influences the soul, in fact it always happens according to the norms of nature, pre-existing in an immutable way in the uncreated wisdom of God, which is unreceptive in space; and being immutable, she orders all perishable things, since none of these would exist if they had not been created by her 9. That lambs and not rods are born from the sheep is the work of the immutable and indivisible intelligence and wisdom of God, by whom all things have been created; but it was the soul of the pregnant sheep that, upon contemplating the varied rods, transmitted this polychromy to the fetus that was born in its womb; and all this happens according to the law impressed on the soul by the mysterious power of the Maker. It would be long and unnecessary to reason here about the virtue of the soul in the immutation and lordship of corporeal matter. Hence men, when they prophesy, sometimes announce in their own name the decrees of Yahweh, and then use the formula: This is what the Lord says; or: The Lord said; Others, without such a preamble, usurp the very person of God, as in these words of the psalmist: I will give you understanding and I will set you on the path to follow. And so, not only with words, but also with symbolic actions, it is imposed on the prophet to signify the person of God; as represented by the one who divided his cloak into twelve parts and gave ten of them to the servant of King Solomon, future monarch of Israel. 12 With the same meaning, something already existing in earthly nature, but different from the person of the prophet, is sometimes used with the same meaning, as Jacob did when he woke up, having seen a dream, with the stone that had served as his pillow. Sometimes the symbolic form subsists for a certain time, like the bronze serpent raised in the desert or writing; but there are occasions in which it vanishes instantly, like the bread that is kneaded for this purpose and is consumed in the reception of the Sacrament 13. 20. But since these, because they are the work of mortals, are known to men, they can be honored with religious worship, but not admired as prodigies. The more difficult and mysterious the actions of angels are, the more admirable they seem to us, even though for them they are ordinary and easy actions. The angel speaks as if he were the very person of the Lord and says: I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob; but the Scripture had said beforehand: And the angel of the Lord appeared to him. And the man speaks in the person of the Lord and exclaims: Hear, my people, and I will speak to you; Hear, Israel, and I will indoctrinate you: I am your God. The wand was taken as a symbol and with angelic power it was turned into a snake; and, man lacking such power, with symbolic significance, he consecrates a stone in testimony 14. Between the action of the angel and the action of man there is a notable difference: the former demands our assent and excites our admiration, the latter only asks for our understanding. The object symbolized by both may perhaps be the same. Cf. 3 Kings 11, 3031. The word bread means in this passage the accidents of bread, which, when the Sacrament is consumed, disappear.

He blessed his one death, and to work our double resurrection he put before it and proposed his one resurrection as a sacrament and example. Christ was not a sinner or an ungodly person, so that he needed to be renewed according to the inner man, as if he were a dead spirit, nor to return to the life of righteousness through penitence; but, clothed in mortal flesh, he dies only in the flesh and is resurrected in the flesh alone, and thus harmonizes it with our double death, being a sacrament of the interior man and an example of the exterior. To the sacrament of our inner man, to signify the death of the soul, refers to that groaning of Christ in the psalm and on the cross: My God, my God, why have you abandoned me? With this voice he harmonizes the word of the Apostle: We know that our old man has been crucified so that the body of sin would be destroyed and we would no longer serve sin. Crucifixion of the inner man is the pain of penitence and a certain salutary rigor of continence, and by this inner death the death of impiety, in which God abandoned us, is annihilated. By this cross the body of sin is fanned so that we do not give our members, as weapons of iniquity, to sin, for if the inner man is renewed day by day, before this renewal it was certainly old. It is within that the Apostle's sentence must be carried out: Put off the old man and put on the new. Sense that clarifies by adding: Therefore, putting away lies, let each one speak the truth. Is it not in the secret of the soul where the righteous strips himself of lies to be able to dwell on the holy mountain of God, who speaks truth in our hearts? The resurrection of the Lord's body is proven to belong to sacrament 5 of our interior resurrection by that passage where, after being resurrected, he says to the woman: Do not touch me, because I have not yet ascended to my Father. The Apostle echoes this mystery when he says: If then you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God: taste the things above. Not touching Christ until he ascends to the Father means that we should not feel about Christ according to the flesh. The death of the Lord in his flesh is an example of death.

That the resurrection of the Lord's body is an example of the resurrection of our external man is evidenced by those words to his disciples: Feel and see, because the spirit has no flesh or bones, as you see that I have. And upon touching his scars one of his disciples exclaims: My Lord and my God! Letting the integrity of his flesh be seen, he established this sentence as true: Not one oabello of your head will perish. How does he first say: Touch me not, because I have not yet ascended to my Father, and then allows himself to be touched by his disciples before ascending to the Father, but because the sacrament of the inner man is hinted there and an example of our external resurrection is offered here? Is there anyone so foolish and divorced from the truth that he dares to say that before his ascension he allowed himself to be touched by his disciples and allowed it to women only after he had ascended to heaven? Saint Paul saw in the resurrection of Christ the type of our bodily resurrection, and that is why he says: First Christ, then those who are Christ's. This passage speaks of the resurrection of the body, and adds: He reformed the body of our vileness according to his glorious body. The single death of our Savior served as salutary medicine for our double death. His resurrection is an example of our double resurrection, since his body provides us with sufficient medicinal remedy in both things, as a sacrament of the inner man and an example of the outer man.

The solar year, with its cycle of twelve months of thirty days each (such is the month established by the ancients after observing the lunar phases), contains the number six. And the value that six has in the first order of numbers, that is, in that of units, from one to ten, sixty has in the order of tens, from ten 8 to a hundred. Therefore sixty days are a fourth part of the year. The six of the first series is multiplied by the first of the second series, that is, six times sixty, and the result is three hundred and sixty days, which correspond exactly to the twelve months of the year. But just as the month is equal to a complete lunar cycle, the year is constituted by the sun in its rotation through the zodiacal signs and, consequently, there are five and a quarter days left for the sun to complete its course and close the year. Four quarters make up a day, which must be intercalated every four years—a leap year—so as not to disturb the order of time °. You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord, insinuating in a certain way that the day begins at night. And just as the first days of creation, because of the future fall of man, were numbered from light to night, these, by virtue of the redemption of man, are numbered from night to dawn. Consequently, from the night of Christ's death until the dawn of his resurrection, there are forty hours, counting the ninth hour. With this number he harmonizes the duration of his life on earth after his resurrection, which was forty days. The use of this number is quite frequent in Scripture to signify the mystery of the perfection of the world, divided into four parts. The number ten also has its perfection, and multiplied by four gives us forty. From the evening of the grave to the dawn of his resurrection there are thirty-six hours, which is precisely the number six squared. It refers to the habit of one to two, the proportion of the most beautiful harmony. Thus, twelve plus twenty-four, relation of the unit to the double, are thirty-six; that is, the entire night, plus the entire next day and the entire night; and this not without the aforementioned mystery. It is not, therefore, absurd to compare the spirit to the day, and the body to the night. The body of the Lord in his death and resurrection was a figure of our spirit and an example for our body. The relationship from one to two also appears in the thirty-six hours, when at twenty-four we add twelve. The reasons why these numbers are mentioned in the Scriptures are very diverse, and perhaps someone will succeed in finding others better than those I proposed, or at least equally probable, and even more probable; but no one, no matter how idiotic and short-sighted he may be, will dare to affirm that these numbers lack mystical meaning in Scripture 12a. Those that I specified I have gleaned from the field of the most venerable authors of the Church, in the careful reading of the divine Scriptures, and others I have deduced from the very similarity of the numbers. No one is learned if he contradicts reason, no one is a Christian if he rejects the Scriptures, no one is a friend of peace if he feels against the Church. On the mysticism of numbers in Saint Augustine, see A. SCHMITT, Mathemútik und Zahlenmystiií: Aurelias Augustinus (1930), p. 353-366.

Adam's sin was the path to death for us. Through one man, says Saint Paul, sin entered the world and through sin death, and so it passed to all men, in which all had sinned15. The devil was the mediator of this path, inciter of sin, author of death. To cause our double death he presented his only one. He died, because of his impiety, in his spirit; in the flesh he could not die; but he incited us to impiety and thereby made us deserve to come to bodily death. We desire one thing by evil suggestion, the other follows us by just condemnation. That is why it is written: God is not the author of death, because He was not the cause of death; However, as a just reward, death was inflicted on the sinner. The judge condemns the prisoner to torture; The cause of the torment is not the justice of the judge, but the merit of the crime. Where the mediator of death pushed us, he did not come, that is, to the death of the body; and it is there where our Lord and God, by an arcane and mysterious disposition of his divine and inscrutable justice, grafted into us the medicinal sap of repentance, which the devil could not deserve. Through a man came death and through a man the resurrection of the dead. Men were eager to avoid the inevitable, that is, the death of the body, and neglected the death of the soul; They wanted to avoid the penalty, not the cause of this penalty. In fact, we care little or nothing about avoiding sin; but we vehemently long to escape death, even if it is never achieved.

Christ himself wanted to be tempted, to become our mediator in temptations with his help and with his example. First he throws the enemy out of the fortress where he tries to enter through all the entrances, and after his baptism, with the seductive temptation in the desert over, he orders him to retreat. He who was dead in the spirit did not manage to triumph over him who was alive in the spirit, and therefore, filled with human deaths, he directs his attacks and his efforts to sow death where it is permitted, that is, in what was mortal, the Mediator taken from us. But where his triumph seemed certain, he was defeated along the entire line, because, by receiving external power to exterminate the Lord's flesh, his internal power, which enslaved us from ancient times, is extinguished. And so, through the single death of a man without a shadow of sin, the bonds of sin were loosed in many dead. The Lord, without owing anything, pays tribute to death so that ours, well deserved, would not harm us. There was no power on earth to take his life; but He, by His will, puts off His flesh; because he who could not die if he so desired, undoubtedly died because he wanted to; and this unjust death leaves powers and principalities defenseless, triumphing over all in his flesh.

But there are very few who remain faithful to him, since the majority recognize and drink with pious humility in the spring of his price, and courageously abandon their enemy and confidently run to their Redeemer. The devil himself does not know by what paths the sublime wisdom of God, strong and gentle, can use his snares and his fury for the salvation of the faithful, starting from an upper end, the beginning of the spiritual creature, until reaching the lower edge, which is the death of the body23. The wisdom of God swells everything with its extreme purity, and there is no room for stain in it. The devil, arrogant to a superlative degree due to his immunity from bodily death, prepares another type of death in the eternal fire of hell, where not only spirits clothed in earthly matter, but also those who display an ethereal envelope can be tormented. Proud men, for whom Christ was debased by dying in that sale where he bought us at a great price, cannot avoid this death, a condition of man's ailing nature, and they will also be precipitated with the devil into the eternal. However, in their madness, they put this rebellious angel before Christ, because he abandoned them to a death into which he, because of his nature, did not fall, while, in his great mercy, Christ deigned to descend to it for us. However, they believe they are better than demons and do not stop apostrophizing these cursed ones, immune from the passion of this death for which they despise Christ. Nor do they want to understand how the Word of God, immutable in its essence, could, by reason of its inferior nature, suffer a thousand torments, to which the unclean spirit, because it lacks an earthly body, is not subject. And thus, although they are better than the spirits of evil, they can die in their flesh, something that demons cannot, lacking earthly matter. The divine wisdom of God knows how to extract goods, in a transcendent order, from death and from the devil himself. Villemain has ingeniously defined this procedure of God as an alchemy of Providence. The greater the evil, the greater the good. Without evil the whole would seem less perfect. Redemption is definitive proof of this Aquatinian sentence.

19. And boasting a lot about their victim sacrifices, they do not understand that they sacrifice to the deceitful and arrogant spirits of evil; and if they understand it, they consider the friendship of these perfidious and envious people useful, whose intention is none other than to prevent our return. Nor do they understand how those very proud spirits could not enjoy the honors of sacrifice if it were not due to the only true God, in whose name they claim to be worshiped; nor do they understand how their ritual offering must be offered by a just and holy priest, who must apply it to the intention of those for whom it is offered, and how the victim must be blameless so that it can be offered as purification for sinners. This is the desire of all who want sacrifices offered to God for them. And what priest is more holy and just than the only Son of God, since he has no need to first offer sacrifice for his sin, neither of origin nor those added to human life? On the other hand, what victim could man choose more pleasing to God to be sacrificed for him than human flesh? And what flesh is more suitable for sacrifice than mortal flesh? And what purity was capable of purifying man from his filth, if not the flesh immune from all contagion of carnal concupiscence, born in the womb and from the eenus of a virgin? And what meat is so pleasing to him who offers and to him who receives the offering, like the flesh of our sacrifice, made into the body of our Priest? Four elements make up every sacrifice: the one who offers, to whom it is offered, what is offered and for whom it is offered. The only true Mediator reconciles us with God through this peaceful sacrifice, he remains in unity with the one to whom he offers, he becomes one with the one for whom he offers, and the one who offers is what he offers.

20. There are those who believe they can purify themselves by their own efforts to unite and contemplate God: these are muddied by pride. There is no vice that the divine law detests more and that it grants greater lordship to the spirit of pride, mediator of the abysses, obstacle to the summits, if its hidden snares are not avoided by another means or overcome with the cross of the Lord, prefigured in Moses when, with his arms outstretched, he urged for the defeat of the Amalekites, who were trying to prevent the people of God from the journey towards the land of promise. These proud men promise to achieve purification for themselves, because some among them managed with the insight of their intelligence to rise above the creature and glimpse some faint ray of the immutable truth, and they mock Christians who live by faith alone, without ascending to the veins. But what does it profit the proud to contemplate the transmarine homeland in the distance, if he feels ashamed of climbing the log? From the spectacle of creation to the knowledge of transcendent and immutable existence, it would be reason to consult them when they discuss the conversion of perishable things or the order and duration of the centuries. And although with correct logic and valid arguments they prove the absolute dependence of everything temporal on eternal reasons, can they perhaps penetrate the essence of those same reasons and deduce from them how much variety there is in quadrupeds? its seminal creation, the process of its development, the numbers of its reproduction, its birth and decline; the regulating movements of their instinct when they desire or avoid what is agreeable or harmful to their nature? Did they not look for all this, not in immutable wisdom, but in the pages of history or in its spatial and secular evolution, giving faith to what others learned through experience and recorded in their writings? 2S It is no wonder if they failed to investigate such a long series of centuries and if they failed to find a goal in the uncertain path of the human race, which, like a river, slides quickly, dragging the individual in its current towards his own destiny. Historians have never been able to tell us distant events that have never been experienced or written about. Nor have these philosophers, other superiors, contemplated the things that they understood in eternal reasons; Otherwise they would not have been content to inquire as simple historians into past events, but would have predicted the future. They call those who did this soothsayers, we call them prophets.

But I do affirm with complete certainty that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are the same substance, the creator God, and that the omnipotent Trinity acts inseparably. But this cannot be demonstrated in an inseparable way, since the creature is very dissimilar and corporeal to the highest degree. Thus, through our words, which sound sensitively, it is impossible to pronounce the names of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit without using a certain period of time, essential in all syllabic modulation. But in their substance, by which they are, the three are one, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, without temporal movement, over every creature, without intervals of time or space; one and identical 'from eternity to eternity, eternity that does not exist without truth and without love; but in my words the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are separated, since they cannot be pronounced at the same time, and in writing they also occupy a distanced place. And the same thing happens when I name my memory, my understanding or my will, since I relate each name to a faculty; However, each name is the work of the three powers, because there is no name of these without memory, understanding and will fixing on it jointly. The Trinity acts in the voice of the Father, in the flesh of the Son and in the dove of the Holy Spirit, but we appropriate these actions to each of the divine persons. This simile shows us in some way how the Trinity, inseparable in its essence, can manifest itself separately in the sensible creature, and how the undivided action of the Trinity is found in the things that serve to properly represent the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. 31. It comes to the arguments of reason that heretics put forward against the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son, taken from the words "to beget" and "to be begotten"; For just as they are diverse predicates, so they mean, they say, diverse substances, because everything that is predicated of God is predicated, in their opinion, according to the substance. Augustine shows them that not everything that is said about God is said according to the substance, but also according to the relationship, that is, "non ad se, ad aliquid quod ipse non est." Thus the Father says relation to the Son, and Lord says relation to the creature, who serves him submissively. In God all accidents are absolutely excluded, and his nature or essence remains immutable.

They don't even think about what they are. Among the many arguments that the Arians usually use against the Catholic faith is the following sophistry, which they consider to be of great weight. They say: "Whatever is thought or enunciated about God, is preached not according to accidents, but according to substance." Answer: If everything about God that is preached is said according to the substance, then according to the substance it was said: I and the Father are one. And if this is not understood according to the substance, there is already something in God that is not understood according to the substance and, consequently, it is no longer necessary to understand the words begotten and generated according to the substance. It is also stated of the Son: He did not consider it a shame to become equal to God. I ask: According to what is it equal? If the same is not said according to the substance, admit that in God not everything that is preached is according to the substance. Therefore it is not necessary to understand the words unbegotten and begotten according to the substance. And if they do not accept this conclusion because it is substantial when it is stated about God, then the Son is consubstantial with the Father.

Those who speak this way do not understand that they have a proposition about the term unborn that deserves diligent examination, because not because one is a father is he already unborn, nor is he a father because he is unborn. Consequently, inborn does not say any habit, but is predicated of itself; but, with wonderful blindness, they do not realize that the term generated is relative. One is a son because he has been begotten, and because he was begotten he is a son. The son is related to the father, the begotten is related to the one who begets him; and just as father says relation to the son, he who begets says relation to the begotten. Therefore begetter and unbegotten are, therefore, two different concepts. Because although both things are affirmed of God the Father, the former says habitus to the begotten, that is, to the Son, a truth that the Arians do not deny; but unbegotten, as they affirm, is an absolute term. They say, then: If the Father has something that the Son does not have, and everything that says habit to the subject is substantial, and unbegotten says relation to himself, which cannot be affirmed of the Son; Therefore, according to the substance, he is said to be unbegotten, and thus the Son, since he cannot be called unbegotten, is not of the same substance. This fallacy is responded to by forcing our adversaries to say in what way the Son is equal to the Father, whether in identity of nature or according to his relationship to the Father. Not insofar as it says a relationship to the Father, because the son always says a relationship to the father, and the father is not a son, but a father. The concepts of father and son should not be compared to those of friend and neighbor. The friend says relationship to the friend, and, if they love each other with equal love, the friendship is identical in both. Neighbor also means relationship to neighbor, and since they are equally neighbors—the distance from one to the other is the same—the neighborhood is identical in both. Here the Son does not say a relationship to the Son, but to the Father, and, according to this habituation to the Father, the Son is not equal to the Father. Then what remains is what is only according to nature. And everything that is said about oneself is said according to the substance. Therefore, consubstantiality remains. The same is the essence in both. When it is said of the Father that he is unbegotten, it does not express what he is, but rather what he is not. If we deny the relative in God, it is not denied6 according to the substance, because the relationship is not substance. * Between esse ad and esse in, theologians admit, when it comes to divine relations, an inadequate distinction.
Under no circumstances can an adequate distinction with objective precision be admitted in God, since it is incompatible with his infinite simplicity.

Quia vero relative aio, cum dico: "Filius est"; ad patrem enim refero: relative denied, si dicam: "Níon filius est"; ad parentem enim eamdem negationem refero, volens ostendere quod ei parens non sit. At si quantum valet quod dicitur filius, tantumdem valet quod dicitur genitus, sicut praelocuti sumus: tantumdem ergo valet quod dicitur non genitus, quantum valet quod dicitur non filius. Relative autem negamus dicendo non filius: relative igitur negamus dicendo non genitus. Ingenitus porro quid est, nisi non genitus? Non ergo receditur a relative praedicamento, cum ingenitus dicitur. Sicut enim genitus non ad se ipsum dicitur, sed quod ex genitorfi sit: ita cum dicitur ingenitus, non ad se ipsum dicitur, sed quod ex genitore non sit ostenditur. In eodem tamen praedicamento, quod relativum vocatur, utraque significatio vertítur; quod autem relative pronuntiatur, non indicat substantiam: ita quamvis diversum sit genitus et ingenitus, non indicat diversem substantiam: quia sicut filius ad patrem, et non filius ad non patrem refertur, ita genitus ad genitorem, et non genitus ad non genitorem referatur necesse est.

This being said, if I refer to the substance when I say son, when I say no son, I also deny according to the substance. And just as son is a relative term, since it says habitus to the father, I deny this relationship when I say not son, and then I transfer the denial to the father when I want to indicate that he is not a father. Saying son and saying begotten is the same reality, as we have already proven, and the word not begotten and the expression not son have the same value. We relatively deny when we say: "No is a son," and we relatively deny when we say not begotten. And what does unbegotten mean, but not begotten? One does not move away from the relationship predicament when one says unborn. Engendered says habitus, not to the engendered subject, but to the one who engenders; and thus, when it is said unborn, no habit is indicated to the subject, but it only means the lack of a father. Both meanings therefore belong to the category of relationship. And what is stated according to this predicament does not entail substance; Therefore, although the concepts generated and unbegotten are diverse, they never indicate a diversity of substances; because just as the son says relation to the father and the non-son to the non-father, so it is necessary that begotten says habituation to the generating principle, and not begotten to the non-begenator.

And such is the virtue of this substantive unity in the Father, in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, that everything that is preached in the absolute sense of each one, is not preached in the plural, but in the singular. Thus we say that the Father is God, the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God, and no one doubts that God is substance; However, there are not three gods, but only one God, who is the exalted Trinity. Great is the Father, great is the Son and great is the Holy Spirit; but there are not three great ones, but only one great one. It is written: You alone are the great God, and this is not to be understood exclusively of the Father, as some perversely believe, but also of the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good; However, there are not three good ones, but only one, of whom it was said: No one is good except God alone. To the young man who called him a good Teacher as a man, our Lord Jesus Christ, elevating his thoughts, does not say that no one is good but only the Father, but: No one is good but only God. In the name of Father only the Father is included; but the word God includes the Son and the Holy Spirit, since in the Trinity there is only one God. Accidents of position, habit, time and place can only be predicated of God improperly and in a translational or metaphorical sense. Thus it is said that he is sitting on a cherub, which indicates a certain posture; covered by the seas like a royal mantle, referring to the habit. Your days have no end, we say in relation to time; and: If I rise to heaven, there you are, alluding to the place. Speaking of action, perhaps only God can be said to be action, since only He does without being done, nor is passive power even conceived in Him as a substance, by virtue of which He is God. And thus, omnipotent is the Father, omnipotent is the Son, and omnipotent is the Holy Spirit 8; But there are not three omnipotents, but only one Omnipotent, by whom, in whom and for whom all things are; to Him the glory.

But since in our common speech the word essence and the word substance are taken in the same sense, that is why we do not dare to say one essence and three substances, but rather we say one essence or substance and three persons. 11. And just as we do not say three essences, we do not say three greatnesses or three great ones either. In things that are great by participation in greatness, in which one thing is to be and another to be great, such as a large house, a large mountain or a great spirit; In these things, being great is different from greatness, and greatness is not confused with the big house. But true greatness is that by virtue of which not only is the spacious house great and the lofty mountain great, but because it is the cause of all greatness. In everything else, greatness is one thing and greatness another. Absolute greatness is infinitely more excellent than all participated greatness. God is not great with greatness that is not what He is, as if God participated in greatness when He is great: in this case, greatness would be more perfect than God; but nothing exists greater than God: He is great with the fontal greatness of greatness. And just as we do not say three essences, we also say three greatnesses. For God, being and great being are the same reality. For this reason we do not say three great ones, but rather one great one. God is great not because of participated greatness, but with essential greatness, since He is his own greatness. And this same must be understood of the goodness, the omnipotence, the eternity of God and those attributes of God that can be predicated in their own and direct sense, not in a metaphorical and translational sense. No; By stating that it is a principle, he wanted to imply that he was also the creator, as a principle he is the Father, through whom all things are. Creator says relation to the creature, as lord says habit to the slave. And when we call the Father the beginning, and the Son also the beginning, we do not mean that there are two principles of the creature, because the Father and the Son, in terms of creation, are one single principle, just as they are one Creator and one God. And if whatever, remaining in itself, acts and engenders is the principle of the thing engendered, we cannot deny to the Holy Spirit this property of principle, since we do not exclude him from the appellation of creator; It is written that he acts and remains in himself while he acts, without becoming or transforming into the things he executes. Pay attention to your operations. The manifestation of the Spirit is granted to each one for common use. To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the gift of healing in a Spirit; to another, miracles; to another, prophecy; to. another, discretion of spirits; to another, gift of tongues. It is not, however, a light problem to find out if the Father is also a principle in relation to the Holy Spirit, since it was said: From the Father it proceeds. If so, it is not only the principle of what it generates or does, but also of the person to whom it gives. God? Saying that nothing happens in your essence that you can change. It is a law of every relative accident to imply mutation in the things of which it is predicated. Thus, friend is a relative term, and one does not begin to be a friend until love blossoms. Therefore, a certain change in the will is necessary for the friend to emerge. The currency says relationship when it is considered as a price; However, there was no change in it when it began to be a price or when it began to be a deposit or similar things. If the coin, without mutation on its part, can be a relative term so many times, without there being any change in its form or essence, neither in its beginning nor in its end, with how much more reason can we affirm this same thing about the unchangeable essence of God, so that, although some relationship with the creature is enunciated, and this denomination begins in time, it is understood that nothing varies in the essence of God, but only in the creature as the term of said relationship? Lord, cries the Psalmist, be a refuge for us. The word refuge, applied to God, has a relative meaning, since it refers to us, and it is our refuge when we take refuge in Eil. But is there perhaps something new in His essence that did not exist before we took refuge in Him? A certain mutation happens in us: we were viler before taking refuge in Him, and with His help we become better; In God, however, there is no change. He began to be our father when by his grace we were regenerated, for then the power to be children of God was conferred on us. Our nature changes and is perfected by the adoption of children; At the same time, He begins to be our Father, but without mutation in His essence. What is affirmed in time about God, which was not stated before, is a term of relationship; However, in God it is not an accident, but in us, to whom divine relativity refers and according to which God relatively begins. The righteous man changes when he begins to be a child of God; but—far from our thinking—God does not begin to love in time with a love that did not exist before. In this sense the Apostle says: He who joins a hetera is one body with her. He does not say, "They are one," or "It is one," but adds, "one body." A whole, composed of two sexes, male and female.
