HOW God IS SIMPLE AND MANY SUBSTANCE

8. If you ask in what sense this substance is simple and multiple, note, first of all, how the creature is always multiple, simple in no sense. Thus the corporeal universe certainly has parts: there is a larger part and a smaller part, and the whole is always greater than its parts. Heaven and earth are parts of this universal mass of the world; and the earth alone or the sky alone is itself composed of innumerable parts; and always a third part is less than the other two, and the half less than the whole. And the universe, commonly known by the name of these two parts, heaven and earth, is always greater than heaven or earth separately. And in each body, the magnitude is one thing, the color another, and the figure another. Once the magnitude is reduced, the same color and figure can remain, or the color can be altered and the same figure and expression persevere, or the figure can be changed and the original magnitude and color preserved. And they can at the same time change all the physical properties of a body or change some without the others being altered. These examples prove that corporeal nature is multiple and not simple. Love in the Trinity can have a triple meaning: essential love, common to the three divine persons; notional love in the actual sense, exclusive of the Father and the Son; personal love, exclusive of the Holy Spirit. Cf. SAINT THOMAS, Summa Theol., i, q. 37,

Nahil enim simplex mutabile est; omnis autem creature mutabilis.

The spiritual creature itself, the soul for example, is, in comparison with the body, simpler; but, abstraction made from matter, it is also multiple and not simple. It is, yes, simpler than bodies, since it does not spread its mass throughout the spaces, but is all in the entire body and all in each of its parts; and thus, when a part, no matter how small, experiences any sensation, even if it is not in the entire body, the entire soul perceives it, because it perceives it in its body. whole. However, activity is one thing in the soul, inertia, penetration, memory, desire, fear, joy, sadness are another; and some affections can exist in the essence of the soul without the rest, and some with more intensity than others, and so on in countless others with almost infinite diversity. Therefore it is evident that its nature is not simple, but multiple. Nothing simple is changeable, and every creature is changeable 7.

This discussion is born from that scriptural sentence: Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. The word is oppressed by enormous difficulties when trying to express the ineffable; If we say that Christ is neither the power of God nor the wisdom of God, with impious insolence we resist the Apostle; If we confess that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, but we affirm that the Father is not the father of his power or his wisdom, our impiety is no less, because in this hypothesis he would not be the Father of Christ, since Christ is the wisdom of God and the power of God. But who will dare to say that the Father is not powerful because of his power nor wise because of his wisdom? Or is being one reality in the Father and being wise another, so that he is not wise by his essence, as happens in the human soul, which is sometimes ignorant, other times wise, as mutable by nature and non-summative and perfectly simple? Shall we affirm that the Father is not something absolute in himself, and that not HÓIO as Father, but even as being tells the Son habitus? Then, how will the Son be of the same Hubulnence of the Father, if the latter is not in itself essence or subsistent being, but only in relation to the Son? But with even greater reason it must be affirmed that they are of the same essence, because the Father and the Son are one essence, and the sor Father says habitus, not to himself, but to the Son, whose o'essence he begot and by virtue of which he is all that he is. Neither of the two says a relationship to itself, since both signify mutual habituation. Will it be said, perhaps, that the Father in particular, not only as Father, but as being, says habitation to the Son, while the Son says relation to himself? If so, what is absolute? Is this the essence, perhaps? But the Son is the essence of the Father, as he is also the power and wisdom of the Rotten, and as he is the Word of the Father and the Image of the Father. And if the Son is said to be essence in the absolute sense, the Father would not be essence, but rather the procreator of essence, and thus he would not exist by himself, but through the essence that he engendered, as he is great because of the greatness he engendered. Essence and existence are identified in the ontological regions of the divine being.

No one can give himself existence, since it entails obvious contradiction. Saint Augustine excludes in these noted words all extrinsic causality in God, and thus the essence of God is not generated as if it began in time.

Sed si non esset homo, id est aliqua substantia, non esset qui relative dominus diceretur: et si non esset equus quaedam essentia, non esset quod iu-mentum relative diceretur: ita si nummus non esset aliqua substantia, nec arrha posset relative dici. And if the Image and the Word are not identified with power and wisdom, because those terms are relative and these are absolute, not relative, the Father does not begin to be wise because of the wisdom that he engendered, since the Father cannot say a relationship to wisdom without wisdom saying a relationship to the Father. All relative terms are correlative. It remains, therefore, to affirm that the Son by essence relates to the Father. And from this statement an unsuspected meaning emerges, because essence is not essence; or at least, when we say essence, we do not indicate the essence, but rather the relationship. An example. When you say lord, you do not indicate the essence, but the relationship, since it says habit of the servant; but when it is said man or similar pose, with absolute and not relative meaning, then that is when the essence is indicated. When we call a man sir, the man is the absolute, sir indicates the relationship; man is the essence, lord says habit to the servant; Therefore, if in our matter the essence entails relationship, the essence is not essence. Furthermore, every essence, in a relative sense, is something outside of the relationship: thus man lord and man servant, horse donkey, coin arra, the terms man, horse, coin are not absolute terms and are substances or essences; sir, servant, donkey, arra, have relative meaning. But if the shoulder did not exist, that is, if it did not exist as a substance, the lord would not exist as a relationship; and if the horse were not a substance, it could not be called a pack animal; and if the currency were not substance, it could not be called arra in a relative sense. Therefore, if the Father is not a substantial reality in Himself, there is nothing in Him that says relationship. It does not happen here as when we refer to color to a colored object, because color does not exist in itself, but always in a nuanced body; However, the object whose color is, although it is called colored in relation to its polychrome, as a body has its own existence.

In no way is it to be believed that the Father does not mean! in itself something absolute, but that everything that is preached about Him relates to the Son; and that the Son says habitus to himself and to the Father, because, when he is called exalted greatness and powerful virtue, it is by reference to his being, being at the same time greatness and power of the exalted and powerful Father, by which he is great and omnipotent. It's not like that. but both are substance, and both are one substance.

Just as it would be absurd to say that sapwood is not white, it is absurd to say that wisdom is not wise; and just as sapwood is white in itself, so wisdom in itself is wise. But the candor of the body is not substance; The body is the substance, the candor the quality. A body is white because of its color, for the body being one thing to exist and another to be white. In the body, color is one thing, form another, and these two accidents never exist in themselves, but in some corporeal mass, which is neither form nor color, but formed and colored. Wisdom, however, is wise, and is wise in itself. The soul becomes wise by participation in wisdom, and if it becomes foolish, wisdom persists in itself; and although the soul becomes incipient, it does not change. But it does not happen to one who becomes wise through the participation of wisdom like candor in a white body. When the body changes color, whiteness does not remain, but rather ceases to exist at all. If, then, the Father begot wisdom and is wise through it, and being and being wise are not the same thing for Him, then the Son is His quality, not His offspring, and there will no longer be great simplicity there. But God forbid that it be so; because the essence there is true and extremely simple; being is identified with having. If, then, in God being and knowledge are the same reality, the Father is not wise because of the wisdom engendered; Otherwise, He would not beget wisdom, but it would beget Him. And what else do we mean when we say that in Him being and knowledge are identified, but that He exists for the very reason that He is wise? The cause of his wisdom is the reason for his existence. Therefore, if the wisdom that He engendered is the cause of His knowledge, it will also be the cause of His existence. Which is impossible, except by generation or creation, and no one until today affirmed that wisdom is the generating or creative cause of the Father. Wouldn't this be crazy? Therefore the Father himself is wisdom. The Son is called wisdom of the Father, as he is called light of the Father, that is, light of light, and both one light. And the same is to be understood by the expression "wisdom of wisdom, and both are one wisdom." Then an essence, because the same reality is there being and knowing. What is to wisdom is science, to Virtue is power, to eternity is eternal being, to justice is being just and to magnitude is being great, is being to science.
And since in that simplicity being and knowledge are the same thing, wisdom and essence are also the same reality.

And it was good to speak like this to make it clear, at least in an enigma, what we were trying to express and to answer when we were asked what these three were; since there are three, true faith assures us by telling us that the Father is not the Son and that the Holy Spirit, the Gift of God, is neither the Father nor the Son. When we are asked what these three are, we strive to find a generic or specific name that encompasses all three, and nothing occurs to the soul, because the infinite excellence of divinity transcends the faculty of language. Thought is closer to God than word, and reality is closer than thought. When we say that Jacob is not Abraham, and that Isaac is neither Jacob nor Abraham, we confess that there are three: Abraham.

OF THE HOLY TRINITY

of three bodies or by some other even more general expression. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, since there are three, let us investigate what three they are and what they have in common. It is certainly not common to be a Father, so that they are mutual parents. It can be said that there are three friends, since they are friends relatively and reciprocally. Not so in the Trinity, where only the Father is a father and is not the Father of two sons, but of an only Son; nor are there three sons, because in the Trinity the Father is not a son, nor is the Holy Spirit; nor are there three holy spirits, since neither the Father nor the Son are the Holy Spirit, the Gift of God in the personal sense. What then are these three? If we say that there are three people, the quality of person is common there. This would be, according to common language, its generic or specific name. But where there is no diversity of nature, a generic or specific name can be used in the enunciation of the plural. The difference in nature means that the myrtle, the laurel and the olive tree, or the horse, the ox and the dog, are not designated with a specific word, calling the first three laurels and the second three oxen, but rather it is necessary to designate them with a generic name, saying three trees or three animals. But here, where there is no diversity of essence, it is appropriate that these three people have a specific name, a name that we do not find. Person is a very generic term, and is even applied to man despite the distance between God and the mortal. 8. Furthermore, insisting on this generic expression, if we say three people, because they have this quality of a common person—otherwise they could not be called that, just as we cannot say three children, since filiation is not common in the Trinity—why not say three gods? Certainly there are three persons, because the Father is a person, the Son is a person and the Holy Spirit is a person; If the Father is God, the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God, why aren't there three gods? And if, by virtue of their ineffable union, the three are one God, why not one person, so that we cannot affirm that they are three, although we give each one in particular the name of person, just as we cannot say that they are three gods, although in particular we call the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit God? Is it because three gods are never mentioned in Scripture? But we also do not find that the Scripture speaks of three people.

If the essence is a specific name common to the three divine persons, why not say three essences, just as it is said that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are three men, because it is the specific word of honor common to all three? And if the name essence is not a specific term, but a generic one, with the man, the sheep, the tree, the star and the angel being the essence, why are they not said to be three essences, just as three horses are said to be three animals, and three laurels are three trees, and three stones are three bodies? And if by virtue of 'the intimate union of the Trinity, we do not say three essences, but one essence, why • because of this same union of the Trinity, we do not say three substances or persons, but one substance and one person? The name of essence is as common in the Trinity as that of substance or person. What we, following custom, say about the person, the Greeks understand, according to the genius of their language, about the substance. They say three substances and one essence. We, three persons and one essence or substance 6. 9. What remains for us, then, but to confess that these expressions are part of indigence, when speaking, in numerous disputes, against the insidiousness and errors of heresy? Holy ritual is the Father or the Son. Poverty therefore sought how to express these three things, and called them substances or persons, not wanting to signify with these words any diversity nor anything singular or concrete, implying unity by placing in God an essence, and the Trinity by distinguishing three substances or persons. Because if in God being and subsisting are identified, three substances are not to be imagined, just as three essences are not said to be; and since being and knowledge are the same reality for God, it is not said that there are three essences or three wisdoms in Him. And since being and being God are identified in God, it is not permitted to say three essences or three gods. If for God being is one thing and subsistence is another, as it is one thing to be God and another to be Father or Lord, being is predicated of the subject, Father says relation to the Son, Lord to the servant; then subsistence would be a relative term, as the term engender is relative and lordship is also relative. And then the substance would not be substance, but relationship. Just as the word essence is derived from the verb to be, the term substance comes from the verb to subsist. It is, therefore, absurd to give a relative meaning to the word substance; Because, if every being is subsistent in itself, how much more reason is God not subsistent?

10. Is subsistence a word worthy of God? Its meaning is well understood in the realities that serve as subjects for others, such as color or shape in bodies. The body subsists, and that is why it is substance; but the color or the form subsists as a proper subject in the body, and, therefore, they are not substances, but subsist in the body, which is a substance. If said color or shape disappears, it does not prevent the body from being a body, since for it being of a certain color and existing are not the same thing. We properly call mutable and composite beings substances. If God subsists and can be properly called substance, something exists in Him as a subject, and then it would no longer be simple, for the being and its attributes are not identified in Him, as great, good, omnipotent and any other.

Is it that certain signs are noticed in the movements of the body by which this or that man shows himself to be righteous? But how does he know that those are signs of a just soul who is completely ignorant of what the just is? Then he knows it. And where did those of us who are not yet just learn what a righteous person is? If we know it from something outside ourselves, then we knew it in some body. But this is not belonging to the body. Therefore, in ourselves we know what is right. And if I try to find out what a righteous person is to translate it into words, I do not find any answer anywhere, except within myself; And if I ask another what a righteous person is, he will search within himself for the word, and everyone who gives an adequate answer will find the answer within himself. Thus, when it pleases me to talk about Carthage 12, I look within myself for something to express intent, and in me I discover the image of Carthage, an image that I received through the mediation of the body; that is, from the senses of the body, since I was personally there and saw the city, felt its life and preserve its memory; and so, when I want to speak I can find the word within me. The image imprinted in my memory is his word; not this trisyllabic sound, perceptible when one says Carthage or when in the secret of the soul one thinks of it during a certain interval of time; but the verb that I intuit in my mind when I pronounce this trisyllabic name, and even before I pronounce it. And the same thing happens when I want to talk about Alexandria, a city that I have never visited; because instantly his image appears on the plate of my fantasy. When I heard many praise the great city, I gave them credit and its image remained imprinted on my soul, which is like its verb inside me when I am pleased to name it even before my lips utter its five syllables, a name well known to almost everyone. And if it were possible for me to make her come out of me and present her image to the men who know Alexandria by sight, they would undoubtedly exclaim: "It is not her"; and if they said: "She is," I would be greatly admired, because, when I sensed in my soul her image as a finished painting, I could not recognize that it was her, and I lend faith to those who still retain her image one day seen by them. But this is not how I look for what is right, nor how I find it, nor how I intuit it when I speak; "I arrived in Carthage, and a boil of guilty loves sizzled everywhere around me."

And everyone who listens to me and knowingly agrees, sees this same thing within themselves, although it is not what they intuit either. But, if he who speaks is just, he says and contemplates what is. And where, if not in himself, does he see it? And it is no wonder, because where is he to see himself but within himself? The admirable thing is that the soul sees in itself what it has never seen anywhere, and sees the truth and sees what a truly just soul is, and he who sees all this in himself is a soul, but not a just soul. Is there, perhaps, a just soul in a soul that is not yet just? And if it is not just, what soul does it see in it when it sees and says what a just soul is, since the soul does not see it anywhere else but in itself, even when it is not a just soul? Could what he sees be the inner truth, present to the soul that is capable of intuiting it? But not everyone can see it, and those who can are not all what they see, that is, not everyone is a righteous soul, although they can see and express what a righteous soul is. And how can they become just if not by adhering to the ideal that they see to model themselves on their die and thus be just souls? And not be content with knowing and defining that he is just who orders his life according to the postulates of science and reason and gives to each one what is his, since it is also necessary to strive to live according to justice, being fairly moderated, distributing to each one what is his and owing no one but mutual pleasure. If you love yourself, you must already love something in order for love to be loved. \ Just as the word means something, it also means itself; but the word is not signified, but means that it means something; So does charity, it loves itself; but if one does not love as loving something, one does not love as charity. What does love love, if not what we love with charity? And this something, based on what is closest to us, is our brother. Notice how strongly the apostle Saint John commends fraternal charity: He who loves his brother, he says, is in the light, and there is no scandal in him. It is evident that perfection for the Apostle lies in love for his brother; for he in whom there is no scandal is, without a doubt, perfect. It seems, however, to silence the love of God, something it would never do if the love of God were not included in fraternal charity itself. He says it very clearly shortly after in the same Letter: Dearest friends, let us love each other, because charity comes from God. He who does not love does not know God, because God is charity. The context openly declares that brotherly love—brotherly love is mutual love—is not only the gift of God, but, according to such grave authority, God himself. Consequently, when we love our brother in charity, we love our brother in God; and it is impossible not to love the love that impels us to the love of our brother. From which it follows that those two precepts never exist, one without the other. If God is love, he who loves charity certainly loves God; and it is necessary that he who loves love love his brother. That is why the Apostle adds: He who does not love his brother, whom he sees, cannot love God whom he does not see. And the reason for not seeing God is because he does not love his brother. He who does not love his brother is not in charity, and he who is not in charity is not in God, because God is love. And he who is not in God is not in the light, because God is light and in Him there is no darkness. And he who does not live in the light. What wonder that he does not see the light, that is, he does not see God, since he is in darkness? You can know your brother by sight, but not God. If you loved the one you see in human appearance with spiritual love, you would see God, who is charity, as it is possible to see Him with your inner gaze. Why do we, when reading this, burn with love for the apostle Saint Paul, if not because we believe that he lived like this? And from what we see we love the one we believe lived like this; and if we did not primarily love the model, always permanent and unchangeable in our gaze, it would not love." The psychological law that explains all the movements of the soul is for Saint Augustine love. Amor meits pondus meum. The first words of his wonderful rule recommend, ante omnia, the love of God and the love of neighbor. Brothers in religion must have one heart and one soul in God. These forms, if they are present, we perceive them through the sense of the body; of the absent ones we remember their images archived in memory, or, according to the law of similarities, we pretend them just as we would create them in reality if we had the means and the will. WE CONCEIVE AND INNERLY GENDER A VERB WHEN CONTEMPLATING THINGS IN THE ETERNAL TRUTH

12. With the gaze of the soul we see in this eternal Truth, by which all temporal things have been created, a form that is a model of our existence and of everything we act in ourselves or in the bodies, when acting according to true and right reason: through it we conceive a true news of things, which is like a verb generated within us when we speak, and which when born does not depart from us. And when we address the word to others, we add to our inner verb the ministry of the voice or some other sensitive sign, in order to produce in the soul of the listener, through a material memory, something very similar to what remains in the soul of the speaker. Thus, we do nothing for the members of the body, neither in words nor in deeds, in approving or rebuking the moral conduct of men, without the secret word being anticipated within us. No one willingly does something without first speaking it in their heart.

Sometimes we admire the results of these sciences because we have heard them praised or from our own experience, and we become inflamed with the desire to learn with the hope of reaching that goal. It is as if an illiterate person were told that there is an art, available to everyone, by means of which one can send silent, hand-drawn words to a person who lives very far away, and the person to whom they are addressed understands them, not with his ears, but with his eyes, and verifies that this is true: would he not direct his efforts to this already known goal if he wanted to learn to write? In this way the spirits of the apprentices are inflamed; because what is absolutely unknown, can under no circumstances be loved. 2. And the same thing happens if someone hears an unknown sound, for example, that of a word whose meaning he does not know and longs to know; that is, he wants to know the object designated by said sound. Suppose you hear the word temetum 1 and, in your ignorance, ask what it means. It is necessary to already know that it is a sign; that is, not an empty sound, but full of meaning; Furthermore, this trisyllable is already known, and through the sense of hearing, its news was imprinted on the soul when spelled. What more can be required for its greater knowledge, if we are familiar with all its letters and all the spaces of its sounds, but because at the same time we know that it is a sign and we are spurred by the desire to know what object it is a sign of? The more one knows, without reaching full knowledge, the more the soul yearns to know what remains. If someone knew only the existence of this word and was unaware that it was a sign of some reality, they would suspend their search, already content with their sensitive perception. But since he now knows not only that it is a word, but also a sign, he longs for its perfect knowledge. No sign is fully known if we do not know what it is a sign. And he who with ardent diligence studies to know and is inflamed and perseveres in his effort, will he be fasting from love? What then is it that I love? It is not possible, in truth, to love a thing without knowing it. He who already knows them does not love these three syllables. Therefore, all love of the studious soul, that is, eager to know what it does not know, is not love of something unknown, but known, and for it it longs to know what it does not know. And if he is so curious that only the desire to know spurs him on, not another known cause, this curious person of ours must be discerned from the true student, but even so he does not love the unknown, but more properly we would say that he hates the unknown, since ignorance abhors him who desires to know everything. But if someone proposes another more difficult question to us, saying that it is as impossible to hate what is unknown as it is to love what is unknown, I will not do violence to the truth; but it is not the same to say: "He loves to know what he does not know", and to affirm: "He loves the unknown." It is possible that there is someone who loves to know what he does not know, but no one loves the unknown. The verb know is not used without reason, because he who desires to know what he does not know, loves knowledge, he does not know it. Without this knowledge I could not firmly say what I don't know or what I know. It is, therefore, necessary for him to know what knowledge is, not only for he who says: "I know," and tells the truth, but even for he who says: "I don't know," and affirms it with poise and truth, and knows that he is telling the truth, and knows what it is to know; for he distinguishes the ignorant from the wise when, examining himself, he says with sincerity: "I do not know"; When you know that you are telling the truth, how do you know it, if you don't know what knowledge is?

And if he finds it similar to the image that fame proclaims, to which he can truly say: "I already loved you," he did not even then love the unknown, since it was already known to him in this likeness. Or we see and love something in the splendor of everlasting reason and when, reproduced in the image of a temporal object, it is offered to our faith and our love through the praise of those who have experienced it, we love nothing unknown, as I proved above; or we love something known, and this drives us to inquire into what is unknown; then it is not the unknown that is the object of our love, but rather the known, to which we know we belong in order to know that which, even though unknown, we seek, as I saw recently when speaking of the secret word. Or, finally, one loves knowledge, a truth that no one thirsty for science can ignore. For these reasons, those who long to know the unknown seem to love the unknown: but these, due to their ardent desire to learn, cannot be said to be without love. I believe I have shown contemplators of the truth that this is not the case, since it is impossible to love what is unknown. But since the examples given refer only to those who long to know realities outside themselves, let us see if any novelty arises when it is the mind that longs to know itself.

I remember that I have memory, intelligence and will; I understand that I understand, I want and I remember; I want to love, remember and understand, and at the same time I remember all my memory, intelligence and will. What I don't remember from my memory is not in my memory. Nothing in my memory exists as present as memory. Then I remember it in its entirety. In the same way I know that I understand everything I understand, I know that I want everything I want, I remember everything I know. Therefore, I remember all my intelligence and all my will. Likewise, I understand these three things, and I understand them all at the same time. Nothing intelligible exists that I do not understand, but what I do not know. What I don't know, I neither remember nor want. Consequently, whatever I do not understand and is intelligible, I neither remember nor love. On the contrary, everything intelligible that I remember and love is understandable to me. My will, whenever I use what I understand and remember, encompasses all my intelligence and all my memory. In conclusion, as each and every one mutually understands each other, there is equality between the whole and the part, and the three are unity: one life, one mind, one essence. This text is considered by the Augustinians of! medieval period as decisive to prove the absolute identification between the soul and its faculties. This essential unity is required by the theory of the soul as an image of the Trinity. The constitution of the human spirit is wonderfully analogous to the mystery of the divine Trinity, and this mystery penetrates the constitution of the human spirit.

Memory, understanding and will are like terms of three real relationships in one essence. The resemblance to the Trinity is drawn with sharp outlines. One essence and three people: one essence and three faculties.

Let us seek in this corruptible man, to the extent of our possibilities, an effigy of the Trinity, which, if less perfect, is perhaps easier to recognize. He would be called man without reason if he did not offer some resemblance to the inner man. Our condition as carnal and mortal men makes the study of visible things more accessible and familiar than that of intelligible things: the former are external, the latter interior; We perceive those through the senses of the body, these with our intelligence; We ourselves are souls, but not sensible, that is, bodies, but intelligible, since we are life. However, such is, as I said, our familiarity with matter, that our attention looks outside with astonishing ease, and thus, when it has to tear itself away from the uncertainty of matter to fix its attention, with more firmness and certain knowledge, on the spirit, it takes refuge in these things, and seeks its rest where its illness originated. We must temper ourselves with this weakness of ours, and so, when we want to distinguish more comfortably the interior and spiritual realities and convince more easily, we must take our arguments and analogies from the external world of bodies. The external man, endowed with a sensitive body, perceives bodies; and in this sense it is subdivided, as is easy to see, into five: sight, smell, taste, hearing and touch. But it would be superfluous and unnecessary to interrogate all these five senses for what we are looking for. What one tells us, the others confirm. Let us therefore preferably use the testimony of sight. It is the noblest bodily sense and the closest, except for gender differences, to the vision of the mind.

It is, therefore, the vision engendered by a visible object, but never alone, but in the presence of a seer. Consequently, vision is engendered by a visible object and a subject that sees: the sense of sight and the attention with which it looks and contemplates belong to the subject; The information of the sense that is called vision, is the work of the body that is seen, that is, of the visible object. Once this is removed, the printed form lacks existence in the sense while the visible object was present; However, the sense remains, which already existed before perceiving anything. It happens as with the imprint of a body in water: the imprint subsists as long as the body that imprints it acts; fades when removed; but the water, which already existed before receiving the imprint, endures. Consequently, we cannot say that the visible body engenders sense, but it does engender a certain form, as a likeness of its own, which acts in sense when perceiving an object with sight. But sense cannot distinguish the form of the visible body from the printed form in the sense of the seeing subject; because the union is so great that distinction has no place. However, reason teaches us that vision would be impossible if a similarity of the contemplated object did not occur in our sense. When applying a cameo to the wax, the non-existence of its image cannot be affirmed, although it is only discernible after separation. But since when the wax is separated the impression of the image remains visible, it follows that the relief was already printed before the separation occurred.

5. Let us remember—for this is so—that these three things, namely, the visible image of the body, its image impressed in the sense, which is vision and informed sense, and the will of the mind applying the sense where vision is verified to the sensible object, although of a very different nature, are tempered in a certain unity. The first of these three elements, that is, the visible objective, never belongs—except when we contemplate our body—to the nature of the animate being. The second belongs in such a way that it acts in the body and through the body in the soul, since it has a place in the sense that without the body and the soul it does not exist. The third, which is the will, is exclusive to the soul. And since these three realities are so different in nature, however, they come together in such an intimate unity that the first two, namely, the image of the visible body and the image formed in the sense, called vision, are barely discernible if reason does not intervene as judge. The will has such power to unite these two realities, that it applies to the visible object the meaning to be informed and retains it in it once informed. And when it is so violent that it can be called love, greed or libido, then it disturbs with great vehemence the entire body of the animated being; and if a harder and more inert material does not resist him, it changes him in the species and color he contemplates. Look at the tiny chameleon how it transforms with admirable ease into the colors it sees 3. In other animals, whose corpulence does not lend itself to these mutations, fetuses reveal, discovering the lustful desires of their mothers, the objects that they looked at with great delight. And the more tender and, so to speak, the more formable these primordial seeds are, the more docility and effectiveness they follow the intention of the maternal soul, adapting to the image left in its fantasy by the object that it gazed upon with passionate covetousness. We could add numerous examples; but one suffices, taken from the most faithful Books, that of Jacob, who, to ensure that his sheep and goats gave birth to spotted offspring, placed bundles of polychrome rods in the watering troughs, and thus, when approaching to drink, at the moment of impregnation, they looked at them. According to the ancients, the polychromy of the shy and heavy chameleon obeyed internal impulses of anger, affection, envy, etc. Today we know that it is a surprising case of variable mimicry.

But the rational soul is deformed when it lives according to the trinity of the external man; that is, when it is given to external things, which form the corporeal sense, not with the laudable intention of referring them to a useful end, but rather carried away by a clumsy desire that leads it to cling to them. And thus arises the trinity composed of memory, inner vision and will, which unites the two. And, when these three things come together in unity, their meeting is called thought 4. And the more vehement the desire or fear, the clearer the gaze acted by the sensitive object, whether it is in the space located, whether it arises in the thinking subject from the image of the body that memory treasures.

What the presence in the place of an object is to the body's sense, is to the soul's gaze the image of the object in memory; and what is the vision of the one who looks at the corporeal species that informs the sense, is the vision of the one who thinks of the image of the object in the memory formed, from which the gaze of the soul is born; Finally, it is, in this passage, the imagination, the internal sense that preserves the images perceived by the external senses and reproduces and combines them according to the laws of association, which modern psychiatry classifies into the law of succession, simultaneity, similarity, contrast and logical connection, all reducible to that of contiguity. Due to its intervention in the passionate and sensitive life, it presents dangers for the heart, whose passions it fuels, and for the individual's personal character.

But neither is she a true father, nor is this her true offspring. The gaze of the soul 9, informed by memory when we remember something, does not proceed in that way that we remember having seen—although we could not remember it if we had not seen it—, but before seeing the body that we remember there was the gaze of the soul that is formed by remembering, and even more so it already existed before recording it in memory. However, the form that is born in the gaze of memory comes from that which exists immanently in memory; Despite this, the inner gaze does not bring its existence from it, since it already existed before receiving this form. And logically, if she is not a true father, neither will this be her legitimate offspring. But that quasi-father and this quasi-offspring hint at something; They exercise us to see more intimate and true things with more certainty and security. 12. It is difficult to discern whether the will, which unites memory with vision, is the parent or offspring of either of the two, and the difficulty of this distinction comes from the evenness and equality of its nature and substance. Here it does not happen as in the external world, where it is easy to distinguish the sensible body from the informed sense and the will from one and the other, because of the diversity of nature that, as we sufficiently prove, exists between the three. Although this trinity of which we are now dealing has been introduced from the outside into the soul, it acts within and there is nothing in it that is foreign to the nature of the soul. How, then, can we demonstrate that the will is neither quasi-parent nor quasi-progeny of the corporeal image that memory retains or of that which is formed in recollection, when the will links the two in such a way in thought that it seems to form only one, to such a point that their distinction would be impossible if it were not for intelligence? And it should be noted, first of all, that it is not possible to have the will to remember not to preserve in the recesses of memory all or at least a part of what we want to remember.

There is no will to remember Intelligence informs knowledge and, through reflection on the truths latent in the treasure of memory, expresses the inner verb, which is like science of science and vision of vision, a reflection of the virtual intelligence that represents the mirror nature of the soul illuminated by God. We must not give credence to those who say of the Samian Pythagoras that he remembered certain sensations experienced when he lived in another body: there are those who put identical experiences in others. These are false reminiscences, such as those we frequently experience in dreams, when we seem to remember having seen or done what we have not actually seen or done. These same affections are produced in the souls of those who are wide awake, under the influence of evil and fallacious spirits, whose job is to strengthen or sow erroneous doctrines about the emigration of souls with the exclusive purpose of deceiving men. If things seen in the world were actually remembered, when living in other bodies, all or almost all of us would have these experiences; because, according to this opinion, a continuous flow and ebb is feigned from life to death and from death to life, from wakefulness to sleep and from sleep to wakefulness. 25. If, then, the true distinction between wisdom and science lies in referring the intellectual knowledge of eternal realities to wisdom, and to science the rational knowledge of temporal ones, it is not difficult to discern which of the two should be given precedence and which should be given last place. And if there is some other characteristic note by which these two things are distinguished, because there is certainly a manifest distinction between them, as the Apostle teaches when he says: To one has been given by the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit, yet the difference we have pointed out is evident, since one thing is the intellective knowledge of the eternal, and another is the rational science of the obsolete, and no one will hesitate to give his preferences to the former.

But, leaving aside what belongs to the external man, when we elevate ourselves internally above what is common to us with animals, before arriving at the knowledge of the intelligible and supreme realities, which are eternal, we find ourselves with the rational knowledge of temporal things. If possible, let us discover in this knowledge a kind of trinity, as we discover it in the senses of the body and in those images that through its lattices appear to us.

On the agreed day, a crowded crowd, in the midst of profound silence, with bated breath and expectant anxiety, hears the graceful mime cry from the stage: "You want to buy low and sell high." How then does everyone passionately love what not everyone knows? Who, as I have proven in previous books, can love what he does not know? How does everyone love happiness, and yet not everyone knows it? Does everyone know what it is, but not everyone knows where it is, and hence the diversity of opinions? It is as if it were some place in this world where everyone who wants to live happily must want to live, and one does not inquire where happiness is, as one inquires into its essence. Because, if happiness consists in the pleasures of the body, he is happy who revels in the voluptuousness of the flesh; if in the virtue of the soul, whoever enjoys it; If in both, whoever tastes both. But when one says: "To live happily is to take pleasure in the whims of the body"; another: "To live happily is to enjoy the virtue of the spirit." Do they both ignore what a happy life is, or do they both not know it? So how do they both love her, if no one can love what they don't know? Is the principle that we establish as true and uncontested when we affirm that all men want to live happily be false? If the blessed life consists, for example, in living according to the virtue of the soul, does someone who does not want to live that way want to live happily? Wouldn't it be more accurate to say: "This man does not want to live happily, because he does not want to live according to virtue, the only happy life"? Therefore, not everyone loves to live happily, or rather, very few desire it, if living happily consists of living according to the virtue of the soul, something that many do not want. Could the principle that the academic Cicero did not doubt be false—academics doubt everything—when, attempting to establish a certain basis where doubt was not possible, he begins his dialogue entitled Hortcnsio with these words: "Certainly we all want to be happy"? Far be it from us to affirm its falsehood. What to say then? Can it be maintained that living happily is living according to the virtue of the spirit, and yet, he who does not want this, wants to live happily? It seems blatantly absurd. It would be equivalent to saying: "He who does not want to live happily, wants to live happily." Who can hear and endure such obvious contradiction? However, necessity forces this if it is true that everyone loves a happy life and not everyone longs to live as one can only live happily.

When he who remained good and faithful in the midst of misery passes from this life to prosperity, he will achieve what he cannot achieve now; that is, live as you want. In that happiness he will not want to live badly, nor will he want something that does not exist, nor will he lack anything that he longs for. You will have what you love and you will not want what you do not have. Everything that exists there is good, and the supreme God will be the supreme good and with his presence he will owe his lovers, having, to top it all off, the certainty of his eternity. There were, it is true, philosophers who pretended for their own use a kind of happy life, as if they could, through their efforts, live as they pleased, a fruit forbidden to the common condition of men. They knew that no one is happy if they do not have what they want or if they suffer against their will. Who would not wish to have in his hand the delightful life, which. happy flame, lasting for eternity? But who is this? Who wants to suffer the inconveniences that must be endured manfully, even if they want to and can tolerate them, given that they already suffer them? Who wants to live in torment, even though he can live laudably in them, acquiring justice with his patience? All those who have suffered these evils, with longings to love or fears of loss, clumsy or laudable end, always considered them as transitory. Many, through these temporary evils, headed, with a strong spirit, towards eternal goods. Hope made them happy in the midst of their ephemeral sufferings, a step to climb the abode of good that does not pass away.

Those whom he first calls sinners, then he calls enemies of God; those whom he first says justified by the blood of Jesus Christ, then he says reconciled by the death of the Son of God; and those whom He says before saved from wrath through Him, later saved in their life. Before receiving this grace we were not vulgar sinners, but we were mired in such crimes that made us enemies of God. Above, the same Apostle called us sinners and enemies of God, but with different names: one very mild, the other atrocious. 15. But what does justified by his blood mean? Tell me: what virtue, I ask, does this blood have so that believers are justified by it? What does it mean, reconciled by the death of his Son? Had the Son already reconciled himself with us, to the point of deigning to die for us, while the Father was still smoking in his fury and was only appeased on the condition that his Son died for us? What does the same Doctor of the Gentiles say in another place when he writes: What shall we say then to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? Perhaps, if the Father were not appeased by not forgiving his Son, would he give him up for us? Doesn't this sentence seem to contradict the previous one? In the first, the Son dies for us, and the Father is reconciled with us through his death; In this, as if the Father no longer loved him before, he does not forgive his Son for us and he himself gives him up to death for us. But I see in the Father a love of priority. He loved us not only before his Son died for us, but before the creation of the world, the Apostle himself being a witness of this when he says: He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world. This is the Catholic theology of the incarnation of the Word proposed by Saint Augustine.

The same person who made Christ suffer a temporary and undeserved death can no longer hold anyone who is clothed with Christ in eternal death. God proves his love for us in that, while we were sinners, Christ died for us. All the more reason, now justified by his blood, we will be saved from wrath by him. Justified, he says, in his blood. Fully justified by him who has been freed from sin; free from all guilt, because the Son of God, free from sin, died for us. We will be saved from wrath through Him: yes, saved from the wrath of God, which is righteous vengeance. Anger in God is not, as in men, disturbance of the soul. It is the wrath of him of whom it is said in Scripture: You, O Lord of virtues, judge with tranquility. If God's just vengeance receives such a name, what are we to understand by reconciliation, if not the end of his wrath? We were enemies of God, as are the sins of justice; once forgiven, enmities cease; Those whom He justifies are reconciled to the righteous. But before that he loved these his enemies, for he did not spare his own Son, but, even though we were his enemies, he handed him over for us all. The Apostle rightly adds: If, then, while we were still enemies, we have been reconciled to God by the death of his Son, a death by which our sins were forgiven, what is more, once reconciled, we will be saved in his life. Saved in life are those who have been reconciled by death. How can we doubt that he will give life to his friends, if he gave them, being enemies, his death? Not only, he says, but we rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we now receive his reconciliation. Not only, he says, will we be saved, but we will glory, not in ourselves, but in God, and not for ourselves, but for Our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we now receive reconciliation, as we explained above. Then the Apostle adds: "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world and through sin death, so death passed through all men in whom all sinned." And the text continues, where the Apostle speaks at length about the two men: one, the first Adam, who transmitted to his descendants as hereditary evils. of the Western Church.

OTHER GOODS OF THE INCARNATION

22. There are in the incarnation of Christ many other goods that are extremely odious to proud spirits, the contemplation and memory of which is very healthy. It is one of them to make man understand the place he occupies among the beings that God created, since human nature could be so intimately united with God that one person arose from the two substances, and, consequently, from three, God, soul and flesh. And for this reason those swollen and evil spirits, intermediaries of deception under the guise of goodness, do not dare to put themselves before man, although free of flesh. Above all, once the Son of God deigned to die according to the flesh, they no longer wanted to be worshiped as gods because of their immortality. Furthermore, divine grace, being granted to us without any merit of ours, was valued in Christ the man; because not even Christ deserved by his previous merits to be so united to the true God that he came to form a person, that of the Son of God; and at the same moment in which he began to be man he became God: hence the expression The Word became flesh. A third good: human pride, the main obstacle to union with God, was corrected and medicated by the profound humility of God. Through it man knows how far he had distanced himself from God and can better appreciate the therapeutic value of suffering on the path of his return thanks to the help of such a Mediator, who comes, like God, to the aid of men through his divinity, and as a man resembles us in weakness. And then what a sublime example of obedience for us, ruined by an act of disobedience, to see

I, according to what is written: To each of us has been given the manifestation of the spirit for profit: to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; If the difference between wisdom and science is that wisdom refers to divine things and science to human things, I recognize both things in Christ, and with me every believer. And when I read: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, in the Word I see the Son of God and in the flesh I recognize the son of man, and both united in one person of God-Man by an ineffable liberality of grace. The evangelist continues and says: And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only Begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. If we refer grace to science and truth to wisdom, I believe we are not very far from the indicated distinction. Among things born in time, the supreme grace is the union of man with God in unity of person; but in eternal things, the supreme truth is attributed, and rightly so, to the Word of God. All men want to be happy; However, not everyone possesses faith, which purifies hearts and leads to well-being. which results from this transitory faith, contemplation and ardor cannot yet be called the image of God, lest what should be established on the eternal appear to be grounded in the things of time. Nothing eternal is intuited by the human mind when it contemplates its own faith, through which it believes what it does not see. What is not eternal is what will one day cease to exist, when, after this pilgrimage through which we now walk far from the Lord, where walking by faith is a necessity, facial vision occurs. Believing now without seeing, we will deserve to see and we will be glad to arrive at vision by faith. Then there will be no faith, by which we believe things that are not seen; yes the vision of the realities that we now believe. So, although we remember this mortal life, already past, and in our memory we evoke the things that we believed without seeing them, said faith will be classified among past and ephemeral things, not among present and eternal realities. Consequently, this trinity which now consists of the memory, the vision and the love of current and permanent faith, will then be nothing but a finished and past thing. From which it follows that, if this trinity were the image of God, it would be necessary to contemplate it not in permanent realities, but in transitory ones. But God forbid that, since the soul is by nature immortal, and cannot cease to exist from the first moment of its creation 2, what is most noble in it should not endure in immortality. And what is more excellent in her nature than to have been created in the image of God, her Maker? It is not, then, in the memory, in the vision and in the love of a passing faith that the image of God is to be found, but in what remains - always. Such, however, is the force of thought, that not even the mind is in a sense in the presence of itself except when it thinks; and, consequently, nothing is present in the mind except when it is thought about, so that not even the mind, platinotype of everything that is thought, can be in its very presence if it is not thought. I cannot understand how the mind, when it does not think, is not in its presence, since it can never be without it, as if it were one thing and the view it has of itself another. This could be said, without incurring absurdity, of the organ of sight: the eye occupies a certain place in the body, but its gaze encompasses all external objects and extends to the stars; but the eye is not in its presence, since it cannot be seen without a mirror, as we have already said; means that there is no place when the mind, thinking, places itself in the presence of itself. Perhaps, when thinking about seeing, does one part see another, as happens, for example, with the other senses, since the eyes see all our members, as long as they can be placed in front of our gaze? But could one say or imagine a greater absurdity? Where was the mind to withdraw from, if not from itself? And where can one place oneself in its very presence, if not in front of itself? It would not be where it was when it was not in the presence of itself, because by placing itself in one part it would withdraw from the other. But if she emigrated in order to be seen, where will she remain to be seen? Or does it enjoy bilocation and can be there and here, that is, where it can see and be seen: in itself to see, before itself to be seen? When the horoscope of truth is consulted, none of these things answers; and when we think in this way, we think only in the feigned images of bodies, and the mind is not a body, as the very few intelligences who can be consulted, on this point, know the truth with absolute certainty. It remains, therefore, to say that her gaze is something that belongs to her very nature, and, when she thinks of herself, she returns to its presence, not through a movement.

If this is so, then she does not possess these three things: her memory, her thought and her love, but she remembered only herself, and then, when she began to think, she understood herself and loved herself. Therefore let us consider more carefully the example given to prove the difference that exists between not knowing any thing and not thinking about it. It may happen that a man knows something and does not think about it, when his thoughts are fixed on another matter and not on that one. Let's take a man versed in two or more disciplines: when he thinks about one of them, he doesn't think about the other or the others, but he knows them. But can we perhaps rightly say: This musician knows music, but at present he does not understand it because he does not think about it, since at present he understands only geometry, since he thinks about it now? This is an absurd sentence, in my opinion. And what can we say about this other: "This musician certainly knows music, but when he does not think about it he does not love it: he only loves geometry, since he thinks about geometry when he disputes about it"? Isn't that also nonsense? But we say with complete truth: "This one whom we now hear arguing about geometry is an accomplished musician, for he remembers this art, understands it and loves it; but, although he knows and loves it, he does not think of it now, but of geometry, about which he is currently arguing." It is a controversial question whether the virtues by which one lives honestly in this mortality, since they have a beginning in the soul and the soul already existed before acquiring the virtues, will disappear once they have led us to the eternal mansions. To some it seems that they will cease, and their opinion could seem true if it concerns the three cardinal virtues: prudence, fortitude and temperance; but justice is immortal and will sooner be perfected in us than it ceases to exist. Disputing Tullius, an author of great eloquence, about these four virtues, Hortensius says in his dialogue: "If we are allowed, upon emigrating from this life, to live immortally on the islands of the fortunate, as narrated in fables, why do we need eloquence, since there are no judgments there, and what are the virtues themselves for? We will not need force where there is no work or danger; nor justice, since it will not seek the good of others; nor of temperance, moderator of passions that do not exist; nor, finally, will we need prudence, since there is no choice between good and evil. We will be happy with only the knowledge and science of nature, the only praiseworthy good in the life of the gods. Consequently, just as in past things the faculty that retains and remembers them is called memory, so, in relation to the present, as the mind is for itself, the faculty of being present to itself can be called memory without scruple, in order to be able to know each other through its own thought and thus the two realities can be linked by love.

meanings the word spirit has, the Apostle, by spirit of the mind, meant the spirit called mind. Thus, when the same Apostle says: In the dispossession of the body of flesh, he does not intend to mean two different things, as if one thing were the flesh and another the body of flesh (in addition to the flesh there are heavenly bodies and terrestrial bodies), but he called the body that is flesh a body of flesh. Here he called the spirit that is mind the spirit of the mind. In another passage he clearly names it image, precepting the same thing in other words. Put off, he says, the old man, with all its works, and put on the new man, which is constantly renewed to achieve the perfect knowledge of God, according to the image of its Creator. What is read there: Put on the new man, who was created according to God, is meant here when it is said: Put on the new man, who is renewed according to the image of his Maker. There it says according to God; here, according to the image of its Maker. There, in true justice and holiness; here, in the knowledge of God. This renewal and reform of the soul is verified according to God or according to the image of God. It is said according to God, so that no creature is thought of; It is said in the image of God, so that it is understood that said renewal takes place in the image of God, that is, in the mind. Thus we say a man is dead according to the body, not according to the spirit, when the just and faithful servant abandons his corporeal envelope. What do we mean when we say dead according to the body or in the body, but that the body is dead, but not the soul or in the soul? And if we say that it is beautiful or strong according to the body, not according to the spirit, what else do we mean but that it is beautiful or strong in the body, not in the spirit? And so on in a thousand other common expressions. Let us not understand, then, those words: according to the image of its Maker, as if the image according to which it is renewed were another and not the same one that is renewed.

23. True, this renewal is not carried out at the precise moment of conversion, like baptismal renewal, which is instantaneous when sins are forgiven, without a single sin being left unforgiven, regardless of the kind. But just as it is one thing to lack fever and another to recover from the illness caused by fever, and one thing is the extraction of the dart stuck in the flesh and another is the medication for the wound caused by the dart, so here the first cure tends to eliminate the cause of the illness, which is verified by the remission of all sins; The second aims to cure weakness, a slow work in the renewal of this image. This double operation is proven by the reading of Psalm 102: He, it is read, forgives all your iniquities in baptism; and then continues: He heals all your diseases; This is the work of daily growth through the renewal of the image. The Apostle speaks of this renewal with crystal clarity: Although our exterior man, he says, is corrupted, the interior SF. renews from day to day. It is renewed in the knowledge of God, that is, in true justice and holiness, as evidenced by the apostolic testimonies mentioned recently. And he who is renewed in the knowledge of God, in true justice and holiness, as he grows in perfection from day to day, transfers his loves from the temporal to the eternal, from visible things to invisible things, from carnal things to spiritual things, and puts all his effort and diligence in restraining and weakening the passion in the former and in uniting himself with the latter out of charity. And he will achieve it to the extent of divine help. It is God's sentence: Without me you can do nothing. And if the last day of this life surprises one in progress and growth, keeping his faith in the Mediator alive, he will be taken to the presence of that God whom he honored, to receive his perfection from Him, and he will be received by the holy angels, taking up again at the end of the centuries his body, now incorruptible, not destined for Gehenna, but for glory. Or is it that these trinities belonging to our senses or our soul are not believed, they are seen, and, on the other hand, the Trinity, which is God, is not seen, it is believed? If this is so, either its invisible perfections are not intelligible by creation or, if we discover some, we do not see the Trinity in them: so that there are things that we see and others that, although we do not see, it is necessary to believe. It is proven in the book HIV how we see the immutable Good even though we are not this good; and we are warned of this in the XIV when speaking of human wisdom, which comes to us from God. Why not recognize the Trinity there? Is this wisdom, which is God, not understood or loved? Who will affirm this? Who does not see that where there is no science there is no wisdom? Are we to believe that divine wisdom knows all other things, but is ignorant of itself, or that it loves all things and does not love itself? If it is impious and foolish to say or believe absurd sizes, here is the Trinity in wisdom, in its news and in its love. Consequently, we find a trinity in man: the mind, the news that brings him to knowledge and the love with which he loves himself 1. In the understanding, in the memory and in the emotional will Augustine discovers a manifest trinity. But how can memory be the image of the Father, being the principle of the Word, while memory is only the image of the things remembered? Those who reason in this way do not seem to understand Augustine's mind. Memory means initial fertility of understanding, which makes intellection possible.

It is important to never forget that similarities are not arguments, and, although the penetrating gaze of the Doctor of the Trinity discovers certain trilogies in creation, he formally declares the mystery of mysteries unapproachable by reason.

Or that the Holy Spirit only through the Father remembers himself, the Father and the Son, and through the Son he knows the Father and knows himself and the Son, while through himself he loves himself, the Father and the Son; as if the Father were his memory, that of the Son and that of the Holy Spirit; and the Son his intelligence, that of the Father and that of the Holy Spirit; and this his love, and the love of the Father and the Son? Who will have the presumption to feel or affirm such things about the Trinity? If only the Son is there his intelligence, that of the Father and that of the Holy Spirit, we stumble upon the same absurdity, that the Father would not be wise for himself, but for the Son; nor would wisdom beget wisdom, for the Father would be wise because of the wisdom that he begot. Where there is no intelligence there can be no wisdom; Consequently, if the Father does not know himself, but the Son knows the Father, in logical conclusion, the Son makes the Father wise. And if being and being wise are identified in God and his essence is his wisdom, the Son would not receive his essence from the Father, as is the truth, but it would be the Father who would receive the essence of the Son, which is unspeakable absurdity and unheard of falsehood. We reject, contest and discuss this monstrosity in book VII. Therefore God the Father is wise by his own wisdom, and the Son, wisdom of the Father, proceeds from the wisdom that is the Father, by whom the Son was begotten. Consequently, the Father is intelligent because of his essential intelligence; I would not be wise if I were not intelligent; The Son, intelligence of the Father, is engendered by the intelligence that is the Father. And the same can be stated without any problem with memory. How can he be wise who forgets himself or remembers nothing? In conclusion, the Father is wisdom, and wisdom is the Son; The Father has memory of himself, and so does the Son; and just as the Father remembers himself and the Son through his own memory and not through that of the Son, so the Son remembers the Father and himself through his own memory and not through the memory of the Father. Where there is no love, who will say there is wisdom? From which it follows that the Father is his love, as is also his intelligence and his memory.
Here, then, are three realities, memory, intelligence and will or dilection, in that sovereign and immutable essence that is God,

The man should not cover his head, since it is the image and glory of God. The meaning of this expression is specified in book XII. We are transformed, he says; changed from one form to another, passing from a colorless form to a resplendent form; for, although blurred, it is the image of God, and it is the image of his glory; form according to which men have been created, superior to other animals. Of human nature itself it was said: A man should not cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God. And this nature, the most excellent of visible creatures, when its impiety is justified by the Creator, is transformed from its deformity into an image of beauty. Even in impiety itself, the more detestable the sin, the more praiseworthy is nature. And for this reason he adds: from glory to glory: from the glory of creation to the glory of justification. We can also understand the phrase from glory to glory in another sense; that is, from the glory of faith to the glory of vision; from glory by which we are now children of God, to the glory that makes us like Him when we see Him as He is. And by these words: as by the Spirit of the Lord, the Apostle proves that this much desired transformation is a gift of divine grace. 15. These things have been said because of that sentence of the Apostle which says: We now see through a mirror. But he adds: in enigmas; and this is unknown to many who ignore the figures of speech, called in Greek tr o pos, a word that has already taken shape in our language. Just as it is more common to say scheme than figure, the word tropes is also better known than the word figure5. Expressing in romance the names of all the tropes or figures, applying its particular meaning to each word, would be a very risky and difficult undertaking. Some of our interpreters, wanting to avoid the Greek word, where the Apostle says: What has been said by allegory, translate by paraphrasing: What is understood from one thing by another. There are many species of these tropes or allegories, among which is the enigma. It is necessary that the generic definition always includes all its species; Therefore, just as every horse is an animal, but not every animal is a horse, so every enigma is an allegory, but not every allegory is an enigma. What, then, is an allegory, but a trope, where one thing is implied by another, as in that passage from the Letter to the Thessalonians: So let us not sleep like the rest: let us be awake and sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, get drunk at night; But let us, who are of the day, be sober? But this allegory is not an enigma; because, if we are not very slow of wit, the meaning of this passage is obvious. Enigma, to put it in two words, is an obscure allegory, as is the expression from the Proverbs: A leech has three daughters, and others like her. But the Apostle's allegory is real, non-verbal, since it speaks of the two sons of Abraham, one of the slave woman and the other of the free woman, which is not a word, but a fact, and by them he meant the two Testaments. But because not only those who are ignorant of grammar, where tropes are studied, long to know what the Apostle meant when he affirms our present vision in enigmas, but even educated people are interested in the meaning of the enigma, the medium of our current vision, we deepen the meaning of these two sentences: We see, says the Apostle, now through an enigma, and he adds: in an enigma. The phrase is one, because it says: We now see through a mirror, in an enigma. As far as I can see, by mirror I mean the image, and by enigma a dark resemblance, difficult to perceive. And so, in the terms mirror and enigma one can understand any similarity in the Apostle's sense, but appropriate to know God in the way that is now possible; and nothing more apt than that which is rightly called his image. No one, then, should be surprised at our effort to see, in the way that is granted to us in this life, an enigma and through a mirror. If vision were easy, the enigma nord would not be found in this place. But here is the great enigma: not seeing what we cannot help but see. Who does not see his thought and who sees his thought, I am not saying with the eyes of the body, but not even with the inner gaze? Who sees it and who doesn't see it? Thought is a kind of vision of the soul, whether the objects are present and can be contemplated with the eyes of the flesh or perceived through the other senses, whether they are absent and with thought we see their images; now none of this exists, as happens when we think of objects without corporeal consistency or similarity of bodies, such as vices and virtues and even thought itself; now reflect on the knowledge acquired through the study of the liberal arts and sciences; now we think of the higher causes and reasons of all these things, existing in an immutable nature; Now we think about futility and bad or false things, we no longer consent to meaning or err in consent.

17. Let us now talk about the known things that we think about, which exist in our knowledge, although we do not think about them, or they belong to contemplative science, properly called wisdom; now to action, which in the proper sense I said is called science. Both are heritage of the soul, the only image of God. When it comes to the lower one in particular, it should not be named the image of God even if certain resemblances of the Trinity are discovered, as we prove in book XIII. We now speak of the science of man in its entirety, a science by which we know everything we know; true things, without a doubt, because otherwise we would not know them. No one knows error except when he discovers its falsehood; If it knows, it already knows the truth, because it is true that they are false. We speak, therefore, of the known things that we think about, things that are known to us even when we do not think about them. But if we want to mention them, only thinking is possible, because, although the words do not resonate outside, he who thinks always speaks in his heart. We read in the book of Wisdom: They said within themselves, thinking crookedly. He declares what it means to speak inside himself, when he adds thinking. Similar is what is read in the Gospel, when some scribes, hearing the Lord say to the paralytic: Trust, son, your sins are forgiven; They said within themselves: This man is blaspheming. What does it mean within themselves, if they did not think? And the text continues: Jesus knowing their thoughts, said: Why do you think evil in your hearts? This is how Saint Matthew expresses himself. Saint Luke narrates this same episode in the following way: Then the scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying: Who is this that speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but only God? Jesus, knowing their thoughts, answered them and said: What do you think in your hearts? The thinking they said of Wisdom is the thinking they said of the Angel. First, what is the same science that truthfully informs our thinking when we speak what we know, and to what extent can a man, however learned and wise, possess it? With the exception of things that come to the soul through the senses of the body, they are often quite different from how they are seen, so that the fool, oppressed by the surprising similarities, believes himself to be sane, taking inspiration from academic philosophy, which, doubting everything, unfortunately maddens 9; With the exception, then, of the things that the soul receives through the senses of the body, how many realities do we know with as much certainty as our living? Here at least we do not fear being deceived by appearances, because he who is deceived certainly lives; Because in this type of visions there is no place for what is objected to external things, in which the eye can err, as it errs when it sees the oar broken in the water, or the navigator sees the towers moving, and six hundred other examples, all different in reality from what appearances show, because this is not seen with the eyes of the body. We know our living through a very intimate science, and in this an academic cannot object: "Perhaps you sleep and ignore it, and you see in dreams." Who is unaware, in fact, that the visions of those who dream are very similar to the visions of those who are wide awake? Saint Augustine, in various passages, recognizes external experience as a source of knowledge, compatible with the illumination of the mind. For the academic, science in the rigorous sense of the word is impossible. We are never certain that our judgments are in harmony with reality. Carneades and Arcesiilaus were the founders of this philosophical school. Cicero, whom Augustine quotes, spread these ideas in the Latin world.
