But he who is certain of the knowledge of his life does not say: "I know that I am awake," but: "I know that I live." Now he sleeps, now he is awake, he lives. Not in dreams does this science fail; because sleeping and dreaming are the property of the one who lives. And the academic cannot argue against this science by saying: "Perhaps you are out of your mind and are unaware of it, since the hallucinations of the insane are very similar to the visions of the healthy in mind; but he who is insane lives." Against academics he does not affirm: "I know that I am not crazy", but: "I know that I live." He who says: "I know that I live" never errs or lies. J0. Contrast a thousand examples of fallacious visions to him who says: "I know that I live"; He will never waver, for he who errs lives. But if human science were limited to this knowledge, it would be little, unless these certainties are multiplied in each genus so that they cease to be few and reach an indefinite number. He who says: "I know that I live", claims to already know a truth; If he says: "I know that I know that I live", there are already two; and when you are certain of these two truths, a third knowledge arises; and thus, in ascending order, he can add a fourth and a fifth knowledge, and innumerable ones if he is capable of it. But since by singular additions he cannot embrace an indefinite number or speak without measure, there already exists another truth that he understands and expresses with complete certainty, namely: that this is true; and since the figure is without number, it is true that an infinite number cannot be expressed or understood. And the same can be said of the certainties of the will. Who can boldly claim that the mistake of someone who says: "I want to be happy" is possible? And if he adds: "I know that I desire this and I am certain of my knowledge," he can add a third knowledge to these two, since he already knows two truths. And a fourth knowledge can be added by knowing that you know these things, and so on to infinity. Furthermore, if someone says, "I don't want to err," whether he errs or he doesn't err, isn't it true that he doesn't want to err? Who will brazenly dare to say to him: "Perhaps you are deceived?" Well, whatever his error may be, it is true that he is not deceived in not wanting to err. And if he claims to know this, the heart of this Augustinian argument lies in a certainty that the academic cannot challenge. If you doubt, live. The contradiction of radical skepticism is evident. He knew them in the same way, not in any other way, before they were created and after they were finished. How different from this science is ours! The knowledge of God is his own wisdom; wisdom, its very essence or substance. In the wonderful simplicity of its nature, knowing does not differ from being; science and existence are identified, as we have frequently stated in previous books. On the other hand, our science is acceptable and can be recovered, because for us being and knowing are not the same thing: we can exist without knowing it, and we do not always know or like (sapiamus) the things that we once learned. Therefore, just as our science is different from divine science, so our word, born of our science, is extremely dissimilar to the Word of God, born of the essence of the Father; as if we said, of the science or wisdom of the Father; and in a more expressive way: born from the Father-Science and the Father-Wisdom.

Is our word born from our science alone? Don't we often talk about things we don't know? And we speak without hesitation, believing them to be true; and if by chance they are true, they are true in the things we speak of, not in our word; because it cannot be the true verb if it does not arise from a known thing. And in this sense our verb is false, not when we lie, but when we are wrong. In doubt, the verb generated by the reality of which we doubt does not yet exist; It is just a verb of doubt. Although we do not know whether the thing about which our hesitation is based is true, we nevertheless know our doubt, and, in expressing it, our verb is true, since we say what we know. Can't we lie? When we voluntarily and consciously lie, our verb is false; The true verb is that we lie; Well, we do know this. And when we confess our lies, we tell the truth; we say what we know; We know we have lied. But that Word who is God, more powerful than us, cannot lie. He can do nothing but what he sees the Father doing; and he does not speak about himself, because whatever he says comes from the Father, and the Father only speaks his Word; and not being able to lie is the great power of this Word; because in Him there is no room for yes and no; only Yes, yes; No no. But it cannot be called a verb if it is not true. If that's your opinion, I agree with pleasure. When our word is true and, therefore, rightly called a verb, can it not also be called science of science, vision of vision and essence of essence, as is rightly and to the highest degree said of the Word of God? No. And why so? Because in us being and knowledge are not identified. We know many things that live in a certain way through memory and die through oblivion, and although they no longer exist in our knowledge, we, nevertheless, exist, and when our science dies when it is displaced from the soul, we continue living. 25.

It is eternal for the soul to live, eternal the knowledge of its living; But it is not eternal to think about your life or to think about the knowledge of your life, because, when you begin to think about some things, you stop thinking about others, without ceasing to know. From which it is inferred that, if an eternal science is possible in the soul, the thought of that science is not eternal; and if our intimate and true verb can only be expressed by our thought, it follows that only God has an everlasting and coeternal Word with Him. Unless it is said that the very possibility of thinking is already a verb as perpetual as science is perpetual, because that which is known, even if it is not thought, can, nevertheless, be thought. But how can the verb be that which in the vision of thought has not yet been formed? How must it be similar to the science that gives it being, if it does not yet possess its form and is called a verb only because it can have one? • This would be equivalent to saying that it must be called a verb because it can be a verb. But what can be a verb, and is therefore already worthy of the name of a verb? What, I repeat, is this formable, not yet formed, but something of our mind that we with a fickle whim throw from here to there when we think now of one thing and then of another, as we discover it or it comes to us? And it becomes a true verb when what I said was thrown at us with incessant movement makes contact with what we know and by taking on a perfect resemblance it is formed, so that just as a thing is known, it is thought of and pronounced in the heart, that is, without a word or thought of a word, since it undoubtedly belongs to some language. Therefore, even granting—so as not to give the impression that we are arguing about words—that we can call a verb that something of our mind that can be formed by our science before its formation, because it is already, so to speak, formable, who does not see how immense the difference is with the Word of God, which is the form of God and before its formation is not formable, since it cannot exist without form being a simple form and in all things equal to that from which it proceeds and marvelously coeternal with Him? Therefore, so that in God it is not believed that there exists something fickle, as if, being a word, it could receive and return to take a form that it could soon lose and undergo evolution in its amorphousness, that divine Word is not called the thought of God.

Just as we properly give the name wisdom to the unique herb of God, although in a universal sense the Father and the Holy Spirit are wisdom, there we call by appropriation the Holy Spirit love, although in an ecumenical sense the Father and the Son are also love. But the Word of God, that is, the only begotten Son of God, is openly called, by the mouth of the Apostle, the wisdom of God. It says: Cris/o, power of God and wisdom of God. But if with some diligence we scrutinize the writings of the apostle Saint John, we will find some testimony where he calls the Holy Spirit love. After having said: Dearest friends, let us trust each other, because love comes from God, he adds: And everyone who loves is born of God; He who does not love does not know God, because God is love. Here God clearly calls the dilection that he previously claimed to come from God; therefore the dilection is God of God. But since the Son is born of God the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father as well, it is asked, and rightly so, which of the two is the true God in this passage. The Father is certainly God, but not God of God; Consequently, love, God of God, must be the Son or the Holy Spirit. In the following verses, after speaking of the love of God, not because we loved him, but because he loved us and sent his Son, litation for our sins; and after exhorting us to mutual devotion so that God abides in us, since he had defined God as love, he tries to express his thoughts clearly, and adds: We know that we abide in Him in whom He gave us His Spirit. Then the Holy Spirit makes us remain in God and God in us, and this works of love. Therefore, He is the Love-God. Finally, repeating shortly afterwards that God is charity, he then adds: He who abides in love abides in God and God in him. Shortly before he had said: We know that we remain in Him and He in us because he gave us his Spirit. Therefore, the God-Love is the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, if among the gifts of God there is none more excellent than love, and the Holy Spirit is the most exquisite gift of God, what is more consistent than that which comes from God and is God is also charity? And if the love with which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father is an indication of the ineffable communion of both, what is more natural than to properly call love that which is the common Spirit of both? Not only the Holy Spirit is love in that Trinity; Reason understands this and faith healthily believes it; but, for the arguments already adduced, it is not in vain that it is properly called charity. Nor is He alone in the Trinity spirit or holy, because the Father is spirit and spirit is the Son, holy is the Father and holy is the Son, a truth of which piety does not doubt, and yet, not without reason, is called by appropriation the Holy Spirit. Well, it is common to both, it is designated by a name common to both. Otherwise, if in that Trinity only the Holy Spirit is love, the Son would be the son, not only of the Father, but also of the Holy Spirit. In numerous passages it is said and read: Only begotten Son of the Father, without this excluding the truth that assists the Apostle when he says of God the Father: He freed us from the power of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of the Son of his love. He does not say: "Of his Son", something he could affirm with complete certainty, as he rightly often does, but here he pleased to say: Of the Son of his love. Therefore he is the Son of the Holy Spirit if in that Trinity only the Holy Spirit is charity. And if this is a major absurdity, it remains to confess that there, it is not only the Holy Spirit that is charity; but, for the reasons already indicated, it is so called by appropriation. The phrase Of the Son of his love is equivalent to this other: "Of his beloved Son", or, finally, "of the Son of his substance." The love of the Father, in its essence, of ineffable simplicity, is nothing other than its nature or substance, as has already been proven and I will not tire of repeating; consequently, the Son of his love is the begotten of his substance.

38. It is a laughable dialectic that of Eunomiou, father of the Eunomian heretics, who, being powerless to understand and not wanting to believe that the only begotten Word of God, by whom all things were created, was by nature the Son of God, that is, begotten of the substance of the Father, affirmed that he was not the Son of the nature, substance or essence of God, but the Son of his will; implying that the will by which he begot the Son was an accident somewhat similar to what happens in us when we want something that we did not want before; as if this were not a proof of our natural mutability, a mutability that faith forbids us to admit in God. It is written: Many are the thoughts in the mind of a man; but the counsel of the Lord remains eternally, so that we understand and believe that just as God is eternal, his counsel is eternal and, therefore, immutable like Him. And what is said about thoughts can with all truth be affirmed about his wills. Many are the desires of man's heart, but the will of the Lord endures eternally. Some, in order not to call the only begotten Word the Son of the counsel or will of God, said that the Word itself was the counsel or will of the Father. But, in my opinion, it is preferable to say counsel of counsel and will of will, as we say essence of essence and wisdom of wisdom, so as not to fall into the absurdity, already refuted, of those who affirm that the Son makes the Father wise and willful if the Father has neither counsel nor will in his essence. Sharp was the response that a certain man gave to a heretic, when the latter cunningly asked him if God had begotten the Son willingly or against his will; because if he answered: "Against his will," extreme misery would follow in God; 17 Eunomius of Cicimus, who died in 305, one of the literary representatives of Arianism, composed the Apologeiicon and proved the Apology, also an extensive profession of faith that he presented to the emperor Theodosius in the years 381-83. For this reason, the Lord Jesus himself not only gave the Holy Spirit as God, but also received him as a man; for which reason he is called full of grace and the Holy Spirit. Where time does not exist, can we perhaps inquire whether the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father before the birth of the "Son", or whether he had not yet proceeded, and, once the Son was born, could have already proceeded from both: just as, where duration exists, we can examine whether the will is the first to proceed from the human soul to then seek what it finds is called its offspring, and when this is born, the will receives its perfection and rests in its end, converting the longing of the search into joyful love of possession, love that proceeds from the mind that engenders and from the notion engendered, as from father and offspring? Such questions cannot be proposed where nothing begins in time, and, consequently, nothing in time is perfected. Therefore, whoever can understand the timeless generation of the Son in the bosom of the Father, must also understand the timeless procession of the Holy Spirit from both. And whoever can understand what the Son says: As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself, do not interpret it as if the Father gave life to the Son, who already existed, but lacked life, but let him understand that he begot him outside of time, so that the life that the Father gave to the Son by begetting him would be coeternal with the life of the Father, giver of life; Whoever understands this, see how the Father has it in Himself that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Him; Thus he gave to the Son that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from Him, and both without interval of time; and thus it is said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father so that it is understood that it comes from the Father to the Son who also proceeds from the Son. If whatever the Son has, he receives from the Father, then he who proceeds from Him receives the Holy Spirit from the Father. But no one here imagines any notion of time, before and after, because time does not exist there. Wouldn't it be very absurd to call him the son of both, since the behavior of the two provides the Holy Spirit with an essence without a beginning of time and without a mutation of nature, just as generation provides the Son with an essence without a beginning of time and without a mutation of substance?
For this reason, although we do not say that the Holy Spirit has been begotten, we do not dare to call him unbegotten, so that no one maligns in said word two fathers in that Trinity.

and I argued and toiled too much. Lord and my God, my only hope, hear me so that I do not succumb to discouragement and stop looking for you; I always long for your face with ardor. Give me strength for the search, you who made me find you and have given me hope for a more perfect knowledge. Before you are my firmness and my weakness: heal this, preserve that. Before you is my science and my ignorance; If you open it to me, welcome him who enters; If you close the shutter for me, open it for the knocker. Make me remember you, understand you and love you. Increase these gifts in me until my complete reform. I know that it is written: In the many words you are not without sin. If only I would open my lips to preach your word and sing your praises! In this way I would avoid sin and acquire an abundance of merits even in the multitude of my words. That man loved by you will certainly not have advised sin to his true son in faith, when he writes to him: Preach the word, insist in season and out of season. Can it be said that he who opportunely and importunately announced your word, Lord, did not speak much? No, it wasn't much, because everything was necessary. Deliver me, my God, from the multitude of words that I suffer inside me, in my soul, miserable in your presence and welcome to your mercy. When my lips are silent, my thoughts are not silent. And if I only thought about the things that please you, I would not beg you to free me from the abundance of my words. But my thoughts are many; you know them; They are human thoughts, because they are vain. Grant me not to consent to them, but make me able to reject them when I feel their caress; Never allow me to stop asleep in your flattery. Never exercise your power over me or weigh on my actions. With your protective help, let my judgment be safe and my conscience be sheltered from its influence. Speaking of you in his book, known today as Ecclesiasticus, the Wise Man says: We would say many things without ever finishing; be the conclusion of our speech: He is everything. When we arrive in your presence, these many things that we now speak without understanding will cease, and you will remain all in all, and then we will modulate an eternal song, praising you at the same time, all united in you. Lord, God one and God Trinity, what with your help is said in these my books, let yours know; If there is something in them of my harvest, forgive me, Lord, and forgive me yours. So be it.
